Results: The main results of our analysis are summarized in Table REF . It shows the mean precision at one (P@1) for the DrQA baseline and BERT-large on the LAMA probe enriched with different kinds of contextual information. Enriching cloze-style questions with relevant context dramatically improves the performance of BERT: B-ora obtains {{formula:23eb901d-afe8-43f1-8c9d-e00632effac3}} improvement on Google-RE, {{formula:d9f461c6-6fa6-4914-b38d-b23a900c9e92}} on T-REx and {{formula:e7fdab23-4fc0-4fd6-b9f2-94fd53381799}} on SQuAD with respect to using context-free questions (B). This clearly demonstrates BERT's ability to successfully exploit the provided context and act as a machine reader model. Remarkably, no fine-tuning is required to trigger such behaviour.When we rely on TF-IDF retrieved context (B-ret), BERT still performs much better than in the no context setting. Overall, B-ret results are comparable with DrQA on Google-RE and SQuAD and much higher on T-REx. This is particularly surprising given that B-ret, unlike DrQA, did not receive any supervision for this task. Pairwise sign tests across relations show that the improvements for B-ret and B-ora are indeed statistically significant (p-value below 1e-5).Figure REF shows the recall of the IR system, which demonstrates that the answer is not present in many of the retrieved contexts, though often the context is still related to the same topic. Table REF reports a detailed analysis of whether the answer is present in retrieved contexts and how that affects the model's predictions. We observe that most of the gain of B-ret comes from cases in which the context contained the answer. However, there are also cases where the context does not explicitly mention the answer but BERT is still able to utilize the related context to help select the correct answer. Note that an extractive approach (such as DrQA) would have provided an incorrect answer (or no answer) for those cases.
Adversarial Robustness: The B-adv column in Table REF shows the LAMA {{formula:a4018421-c1b7-4a0f-b7e8-66b99e8b5976}} results for BERT for adversarial contexts. BERT is very robust, dropping only 0.5 {{formula:5c72ba04-cf4a-488b-b198-78ea828c573c}} on average from the zero context baseline. However, as shown in Figure REF , this strong performance only occurs when the context and question are processed as two segments using BERT's separator tokens. Using only one segment (that is, simply concatenating the input query and the context) leads to a severe drop of 12.4 {{formula:c8a719c7-395f-4be6-a654-423e77ae4966}} for BERT (a 40.7% relative drop in performance). We also observe a consistent improvement in performance from one segment to two for retrieved and oracle contexts.One possible reason for this phenomenon resides in the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) classifier of BERT, learned with self-supervision during pretraining by training the model to distinguish contiguous (i.e., “next sentence" pairs) from randomly sampled blocks of text. We hypothesize that the MLM task might be influenced by the NSP's output. Thus, BERT might learn to not condition across segments for masked token prediction if the NSP score is low, thereby implicitly detecting irrelevant and noisy contexts. A result that seems in line with this hypothesis is that RoBERTa, which does not use NSP, is more vulnerable to adversarial contexts and the difference between one and two sentences (for RoBERTa separated by the eos token) is much smaller. {{figure:33c334d0-ae6f-4a07-b767-690bc00a4ba9}}{{table:e65a7720-c279-4c6a-ae4b-a8ce2ca56082}}To further investigate this hypothesis, we calculate the number of {{formula:05910fce-bd08-4e4b-874d-76749f0ed10e}} pairs classified by BERT as “next sentence" pairs in LAMA for the different context strategies. These results are shown in Table REF . We see that for B-ret, B-gen and B-ora, NSP classifications are high, suggesting BERT finds the segments to be contiguous, and hence useful to condition upon. However, for B-adv, very few {{formula:fa51fd11-dbee-48fe-aa1a-6c509b14cce3}} pairs are classified as “next sentences", suggesting BERT may condition on them less. Additional evidence for our NSP adversarial robustness hypothesis is given in Figure REF . Here we compute the absolute difference in probability that BERT places on the correct answer upon including context {{formula:a4983344-0613-4d44-9064-1b1e8e32bea3}} , and plot it against NSP probability {{formula:91426d67-06c8-42a4-ad84-8c6f0d9a3bdc}} . We see that for adversarial, retrieved and generated contexts, increasing NSP probability is associated with greater change in true answer probability upon including context.Each context method has different NSP statistics, (e.g. the generated contexts have very high NSP probabilities on average) but the trend is consistent—higher NSP scores co-occur with greater changes in correct answer probability {{figure:00d7e48b-6306-47f3-82f9-fac1a32ad4be}}
Generated context: By generating context from a LM we aim at assessing the performance of a solution purely based on knowledge implicitly stored in the parameters of the underlying neural networks. Although the overall results of B-gen are lower than the context-free baseline, some interesting insights emerge from our analysis. First, generated context improves performance for 13 relations and overall for {{formula:751e4b8c-f697-4d96-968e-69ddb1f55665}} of the questions on T-REx (Table REF ). This demonstrates that autoregressive language models can generate relevant context and potentially serve as unsupervised IR systems. They do, of course, generate also irrelevant or factually wrong information. What is interesting is that BERT associates high NSP probabilities with generated contexts—for BERT, the generation is always a plausible continuation of the question. This inhibits the selective behaviour of BERT with respect to the context, and hurts performance when the generation is noisy, irrelevant or wrong.Table REF shows three examples for the generation of BERT-large for adversarial, generated, retrieved and oracle context-enriched questions. {{table:9b109df1-774e-492d-959b-25fcf9fc2b43}}
Discussion: In this section we discuss some of our findings and their implications.
Re-examining NSP: The Next Sentence Prediction task has been extensively explored , , , with the apparent consensus that it is not helpful for downstream fine-tuning accuracy. Our findings, in contrast, suggest that it is important for robust exploitation of retrieved context for unsupervised tasks. Basing design decisions with a limited set of downstream uses when designing general purpose pre-trained models may well us lead to less flexible models. As a community, we should continue to strive for greater diversity in our criteria and possible use-cases for assessing such models .
Practical Takeaways: Section shows that BERT has a very different behaviour when inputs are processed with one or two segments. Practitioners should thus ensure that they thoroughly ablate segmentation options. The consistent improvement upon including retrieved context also suggests that it may be possible to get performance boosts in many other tasks by the trivial incorporation of retrieved documents, even when such documents are not strictly required for the task. We leave investigating this for future work.
Comparison with : We demonstrate that BERT with retrieved context and no fine-tuning performs on par with DrQA on the LAMA probe, but it is worth discussing this comparison further. Firstly, it is encouraging that an unsupervised system performs just as well as a system that requires significant supervision such as DrQA. We further note that LMs are abstractive models, whereas DrQA is extractive, confined to returning answers that are spans of retrieved context. However, it is worth stating that LAMA only requires single token answers. Generating an arbitrarly long sequence of contiguous tokens from bidirectional LMs like BERT and RoBERTa is not trivial, but extractive QA models handle such cases by considering spans of text of varying lengths. Finally, while we have chosen DrQA as our baseline to compare to recent work, there exist several more sophisticated supervised open-domain QA models that outperform it on a variety of open-domain QA tasks , , .
Unsupervised Question Answering: Our work is part of growing body of work that demonstrate that unsupervised question answering is not only possible, but beginning to reach and even outperform some standard supervised baselines. and demonstrate non-trivial performance on CoQA and SQuAD respectively, and achieve SoTA results using an unsupervised method for multi-choice QA on ARC . Taken together, these recent findings suggest that powerful and flexible unsupervised QA systems could soon be a reality, bringing with them many advantages including avoiding biases that often plague smaller datasets by incorporating knowledge from much larger corpora and greater abilities to combine and abstract pieces of information from different sources.
Conclusion: We demonstrated a simple technique to greatly improve factual unsupervised cloze QA by providing context documents as additional inputs. We used oracle documents to establish an upper bound to this improvement, and found that using off-the-shelf information retrieval is sufficient to achieve performance on par with the supervised DrQA system. We also investigated how brittle language models' factual predictions were to noisy and irrelevant context documents, and found that BERT, when featurized appropriately, is very robust. We provide evidence that this robustness stems from the Next Sentence Prediction pre-training task.

reasoning.step1: Paper A (2212.08043) introduces a constructive process-convolution approach to model non-stationary spatial dependence by allowing the smoothing kernel (i.e., the spatial covariance structure) to vary as a function of location, using spatially evolving ellipses defined by dynamically varying foci and covariance matrices. This method enables the spatial correlation structure to adapt locally, such as aligning with environmental gradients like stream channels in toxic waste data, thereby capturing heterogeneous dependence patterns that stationary models cannot.
reasoning.step2: Paper B (2005.03658) applies a non-stationary Gaussian process model to global climate model-derived 20-year return values for surface temperature, where spatial dependence varies between land and ocean regions due to differing thermal inertia and mixing dynamics. The method uses a log-linear regression to model spatially varying isotropy ranges, with ocean regions exhibiting much longer spatial ranges than land. The result from Paper A — that spatial dependence can be locally structured and anisotropic — directly enables the interpretation in Paper B that the observed difference in spatial range between land and ocean is not merely a statistical artifact but a physical manifestation of non-stationarity, where the spatial correlation structure is shaped by underlying environmental heterogeneity.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: Step 2 depends on Step 1 because the interpretation of the spatially varying isotropy ranges in Paper B (e.g., why ocean ranges are 10x longer than land) cannot be meaningfully explained without the conceptual framework from Paper A that defines non-stationarity as a spatially evolving covariance structure. Paper B observes the phenomenon (differential range), but only Paper A provides the mechanistic explanation: that spatial dependence is not uniform and can be anisotropic and location-dependent, like ellipses aligned with environmental gradients. Without the kernel-evolution framework from Paper A, the difference in range would appear as a mere parameter estimate, not as a physically interpretable spatial pattern.

questionDraft: How can the spatial variation in the range of dependence observed in global temperature return values be explained by a non-stationary covariance structure that adapts locally to environmental heterogeneity?
question: How can the variation in the spatial range of dependence observed in temperature return values across land and ocean regions be explained by a covariance structure that adapts locally to environmental heterogeneity?
answerWithPaperReferences: The variation in the spatial range of dependence observed in temperature return values across land and ocean regions arises because the spatial covariance structure is non-stationary and adapts to environmental heterogeneity. In ocean regions, the thermal inertia and large-scale mixing lead to smoother, more persistent temperature patterns, resulting in much longer spatial ranges of dependence — approximately 12,738 km — compared to land regions, where surface heterogeneity, topography, and boundary layer dynamics create more fragmented and localized temperature correlations, yielding a much shorter range of about 1,321 km [Paper B]. This differential behavior is not merely a statistical outcome but reflects the physical nature of spatial dependence, which can be modeled as a spatially evolving kernel, as demonstrated in non-stationary geostatistical models where the shape and orientation of the covariance structure vary with location, such as ellipses aligned with environmental gradients like stream channels in toxic waste data [Paper A]. The process-convolution framework from Paper A provides the mechanistic basis for understanding why such variation occurs: the spatial dependence structure is not fixed but dynamically shaped by local environmental conditions, allowing the range of correlation to vary meaningfully across different surface types. Thus, the observed difference in isotropy range between land and ocean is a direct manifestation of non-stationary spatial covariance, where the kernel’s anisotropy and scale are modulated by underlying physical processes.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The variation in the spatial range of dependence observed in temperature return values across land and ocean regions occurs because the spatial correlation structure adapts to environmental heterogeneity. Over oceans, large-scale thermal mixing and uniform surface properties lead to smooth, long-range temperature patterns, resulting in a much greater spatial range of dependence — approximately 12,700 km — compared to land regions, where topography, vegetation, soil moisture, and boundary layer effects create localized and fragmented temperature variations, yielding a much shorter range of about 1,300 km. This difference reflects a non-stationary covariance structure, where the scale and anisotropy of spatial dependence are not uniform but vary with location. The spatial correlation is shaped by local environmental conditions, such that the range of influence expands in homogeneous regions (e.g., oceans) and contracts in heterogeneous ones (e.g., land). This means that temperature anomalies at one point can influence distant locations over water but only nearby locations over land, demonstrating that spatial dependence is dynamically modulated by the physical characteristics of the surface.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because it requires two sequential reasoning steps: first, recognizing that spatial dependence can vary with location due to a non-stationary covariance structure (from Paper A), and second, interpreting the observed difference in spatial range between land and ocean as a physical manifestation of that non-stationarity (from Paper B). A single-hop question would ask either about the existence of non-stationarity (Paper A alone) or about the difference in range between land and ocean (Paper B alone). Here, the answer requires combining the mechanistic framework of spatially evolving kernels (Paper A) with the empirical observation of differential range (Paper B) to explain why the range differs — a dependency that cannot be resolved by either paper alone.
bridgeEvidencePaperText:
Non-Stationary Spatial Modeling
abstract: Standard geostatistical models assume stationarity and rely on a variogram model to account for the spatial dependence in the observed data. In some instances, this assumption that the spatial dependence structure is constant throughout the sampling region is clearly violated. We present a spatial model which allows the spatial dependence structure to vary as a function of location. Unlike previous formulations which do not account for uncertainty in the specification of this non-stationarity (eg. Sampson and Guttorp (1992)), we develop a hierarchical model which can incorporate this uncertainty in the resulting inference. The non-stationary spatial dependence is explained through a constructive "process-convolution" approach, which ensures that the resulting covariance structure is valid. We apply this method to an example in toxic waste remediation.
INTRODUCTION: Modeling spatial data with Gaussian processes is the common thread of all geostatistical analyses. Some notable references in this area include Matheron (1963), Journel and Huijbregts (1978), Ripley (1981), Isaaks and Srivastava (1990), and Cressie (1991). A common approach is to model spatial dependence through the covariogram function, so that covariance between any two points depends only on the distance between them. Distance is typically Euclidean, though other metrics are sometimes used.Such a specification yields a stationary random field, which has a distribution that is invariant under spatial shifts. If the field is also invariant under rotations, it is called isotropic. Assuming a field to be stationary and isotropic is natural in some settings, especially when the spatial region of interest is relatively small. Though assuming a stationary model gives sensible results in many applications, cases arise when researchers have found it necessary to develop models that allow for heterogeneous spatial covariance structure (Haas, 1990; Sampson and Guttorp, 1992; Loader and Switzer, 1992; Le and Zidek 1992, 1997). Of these, only Hass (1990) gives a method for fitting a non-stationary spatial model using a single realization from a spatial process, although statements regarding uncertainty are difficult to obtain under this approach. The remaining references above all take advantage of repeated measurements over the spatial locations.In this paper, we propose an alternative model for accounting for heterogeneity in the spatial covariance function, which is based on a moving average specification of a Gaussian process. Inference is carried out using a hierarchical modeling structure so that statements regarding uncertainty may be obtained. A large class of stationary spatial processes may be represented as a moving average of a Gaussian white noise process – a white noise process convolved with some point spread function, or kernel (see Thiébaux and Pedder, 1987, ch. 5, for example). We extend this characterization so that this kernel evolves over spatial location. The following section details this new formulation while Section 3 gives the details of using this specification to model spatial data and applying this approach to data obtained from the Piazza Road Superfund Site. We finish the paper with a brief discussion.
SPECIFYING SPATIAL COVARIANCE: We now give details on this process convolution approach for constructing non-stationary Gaussian processes in two dimensions. We first consider stationary formulations obtained through a moving average specification, and then extend this to allow for processes with covariance structure that slowly changes over space. We consider a couple of approaches for specifying a spatially evolving family of smoothing kernels which, in turn, defines a spatial covariance function for the process.
MOVING AVERAGE PROCESSES: Any stationary Gaussian process {{formula:a3b5fda6-189c-4f39-bf81-655cbba65a48}} which has a correlogram {{formula:b4b16439-7cc6-4639-8fe4-40aa9dd5fea9}} given by {{formula:81c31c71-f9ea-482c-b897-b46115364726}}can be expressed as the convolution of a Gaussian white noise process {{formula:d5d7e92a-e22a-4bc6-99e7-0a5fcafb7cfa}} with convolution kernel {{formula:ff2181f8-f0bc-42a8-9279-57f5cbdebd86}} {{formula:977d9456-6034-4b46-87c9-93dbc463c161}}By a white noise process {{formula:fe7d39e0-279e-444c-8c99-9e447ce88321}} we mean a process for which {{formula:9052118e-2e48-4655-8502-b4bcb0038a0e}}for any subregions {{formula:4faf6b10-fbef-4f2c-8d6d-3754b57297ac}} and {{formula:8fdef29e-cf47-48e9-8ea9-53e9c7124c23}} contained in the plane {{formula:09df45fa-9f38-476b-8f34-c6afde447baf}} .Primarily for analytical tractability and computational convenience, we focus on the two-dimensional standard normal kernel {{formula:aacc5989-1509-4853-8028-0c8fa248041d}}which gives the so-called Gaussian correlation function in two dimensions {{formula:9e670ff2-7b12-4554-91a1-8664d0800cd5}}This isotropic specification can be extended to allow for rotating as well as shrinking and stretching of the coordinate axes. In this case we can represent {{formula:ccaad458-4da4-405c-b123-34f118da55af}} as a bivariate normal kernel with covariance matrix {{formula:bba09a97-1d4d-45ee-94e3-e316828da175}} {{formula:16a3829f-b211-445e-a3a7-6ed34c8c33b2}}which is isotropic if one uses the transformed distance {{formula:f1a67c72-7b82-4859-b5c7-bf002c15cb98}} . Hence, the three parameters that make up {{formula:c433041c-96fd-4a76-9ec1-17e9cca61001}} determine the anisotropy in the spatial correlation.
SPATIALLY EVOLVING KERNELS: To account for non-stationarity, we now allow the smoothing kernel to depend on spatial location {{formula:dc91308f-6f68-478b-927e-c88291fcdf9f}} . We use {{formula:5d0657bd-69c0-4451-b08f-36dad676dbd2}} to denote a kernel which is centered at the point {{formula:0fe0c2a1-c6a5-4e7c-ad1d-4ef4733d83f9}} and whose shape is a function of location {{formula:413b6b28-561a-4b03-b85f-e9eca39ba651}} . Once {{formula:f21e0fdb-4f92-4c9d-9b18-1c0de1b15a1a}} is specified for all {{formula:abe56061-b126-4427-887e-d86aa7b9e327}} , the correlation between two points {{formula:f9308dfe-630a-4747-bbe6-5b39648613c5}} and {{formula:ee4adbd5-2508-4027-ad71-b2a28a2ccf6a}} is then {{formula:f6c2c8df-19bd-4b77-a0ea-a963a79ef27f}}Note that the spatial correlation function is not a correlogram since it is no longer a function of distance alone.Because of the constructive formulation under the moving average specification, the resulting correlation function {{formula:38d09a35-e975-4d57-978e-bc8f2d57595c}} is certain to be positive definite, and the resulting non-stationary process {{formula:5b8de7ba-bbe2-4276-9bec-1dd665288fce}}is certain to be valid – no matter how the family {{formula:9b718bad-e7cb-4171-83ef-1bebec8b4f5d}} is chosen, provided {{formula:09c1444d-0d2c-4a28-8f81-66c15180f547}} . We favor working with the kernels {{formula:127ed061-6fdc-4e5d-8443-1a9cbfb68c7b}} rather than working directly with the correlation function {{formula:79f855bd-05b1-43e4-b23e-5641c492b0f4}} since this makes it difficult to ensure symmetry and positive definiteness for all {{formula:9b471287-5083-4fd0-bc33-f3ad069d1365}} and {{formula:1603fab7-7ea4-4177-a4e0-c2b7a878eb31}} .Of course, we require that some regularity be injected into the formulation by forcing the kernels {{formula:b577c922-ad8c-47a8-bf3d-574fecdeeae0}} to evolve smoothly over space. But first, we focus on the form of the kernels. For the application presented in this paper we define each {{formula:87b0e4c9-d543-4d64-8e8b-7b1df441c32b}} to be a normal kernel centered at {{formula:5eed5603-1b63-44fc-a21c-da80ffde9d03}} with spatially varying covariance matrix {{formula:065d1eb4-7672-46b9-86f4-3d9cdbca2b5d}} . In this case if we parameterize {{formula:7b35bf75-4085-4775-aa8a-89d7dac463d5}} and {{formula:a9e71fc5-5062-4a1c-a0ea-b45e33312ce4}} by {{formula:4f5f8254-4250-4cad-85f3-0541be05956b}}the correlation function is given by the complicated, but easy to compute formula {{formula:d70f0725-0e3d-4f37-9949-61c561f0339d}}where {{formula:51473d92-cf83-48cc-aab4-85f345166716}}In order to assure that the kernels {{formula:35e524c2-a688-44db-8b06-da5cb9aaa1a3}} vary smoothly over space, we parameterize {{formula:9500e8c8-2dd9-458f-b0d3-244a34cdc88b}} , and then allow the parameters to evolve with location. We are currently experimenting with a number of parameterizations, but for this paper we'll focus on a geometrically based specification which readily extends beyond the use of the Gaussian kernels considered here.There is a one to one mapping from a bivariate normal distribution to its one standard deviation ellipse, so we define a spatially varying family of ellipses which, in turn, defines the spatial distribution for {{formula:17b4f178-af28-4b00-80be-78a872e2cb55}} . Let the two focus points in {{formula:e37beddc-b5f1-4de6-b38a-1484ea8bcb50}} {{formula:e805ce3f-95a7-4fbb-a608-d018c762849c}} and {{formula:33e2f2c1-74a7-4177-ad29-f3f653403225}} define an ellipse centered at the origin with fixed area {{formula:b47b8730-ac48-4267-935f-0939c8eb7765}} . This then corresponds to the Gaussian kernel with covariance matrix {{formula:efcb3926-c6a4-4f3e-a32f-a5e88fb9f3b8}} defined by {{formula:fffb31ea-d2a7-49fd-88de-26b9e2a9f2a2}}where {{formula:aa9ccc0f-3cf9-42ce-8e2a-d34037445f87}} , {{formula:c3c741db-25c9-4d39-911c-2cc384caeac7}} , and the parameter {{formula:55c17199-8e40-4684-b4ee-c988689196e9}} serves to scale the kernel. This corresponds to a local scaling and rotation at a given site {{formula:673836f4-a7ea-4494-9084-91cc26dae2fb}} . Now we can define a spatial distribution of kernels by specifying that {{formula:d8554576-ec9f-47b8-bff7-66f338f753c8}} and {{formula:56c3f20e-514b-444b-b054-de3e4134dd92}} are distributed independently, according to independent Gaussian fields, each with covariance function {{formula:599e95d4-3572-44cf-baf8-07f6ca5256f1}} . The resulting kernel is then taken to be centered at location {{formula:b59ecfd2-8cea-4f63-b08d-200b18760c92}} . This means that marginally, {{formula:aaf83fa9-c362-459c-aefc-f596e9961d68}} has a bivariate standard normal distribution for any {{formula:7ab810bb-ead5-4e6f-96dd-0c82ee0e21d6}} . Though any covariance function could be used here, our preference is for something simple, and something that ensures very smooth spatial variation for the ellipses. The choice of {{formula:30b6672d-9dd0-454d-be54-da981a3a5750}} will certainly depend on the application, however the choice of ellipse area {{formula:0ff50629-a1b8-4f49-8f65-b3fddc6c6376}} is something we prefer to fix at a value that gives sensible ellipses when {{formula:836dfdae-fc15-4121-8718-7d29541fc69f}} are drawn from their Gaussian field distributions. After a fair bit of simulation and experimentation, we have settled on {{formula:4536faf2-8a78-4bd5-ab07-e98f6e621733}} . Note that the scale parameter {{formula:b43c236d-70b2-43cb-8c52-16a515eb437f}} controls the size of the kernels {{formula:cf27f84f-b612-4ad9-b70b-e3936e486c5c}} , and hence serves to control the range of spatial dependence of the resulting process {{formula:e7e8f93a-8cc7-4dad-8188-d53dbfc1fe6e}} . {{figure:65c09db4-a9a6-4032-8e35-9f4478908e5e}}Figure 1 shows a spatially evolving sequence of focus points {{formula:83c55e1a-9bff-4d01-b09e-85edac57b98e}} in the upper frame, and shows the resulting ellipses in the lower frame. This demonstrates how the spatially distributed pairs {{formula:7654c0df-f8a9-44a3-b742-32b6db144853}} give rise to a spatially distributed covariance matrix {{formula:8cdecbd2-c9b5-46fa-a592-c768b14d47f4}} . Finally, Figure 2 shows a realization from this non-stationary random field that has just been specified. The first frame shows the ellipses corresponding to the realization {{formula:6a5e38a8-f74a-4161-9395-25280f59d3a2}} drawn from their Gaussian process distributions. Conditional on these kernels, the covariance matrix for a {{formula:af8b60d5-718e-4da0-a597-aa8bec39c94a}} lattice of sites is constructed and a multivariate normal draw is then made. The resulting surface is shown in the second and third frames. Note that the ellipses shown in Figure 2 are shrunken down by a factor of 10 so that they can be seen on the plot. {{figure:7222d216-5e30-4ab5-a7c1-7a58f081f9a7}}
APPLICATION IN ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING: This non-stationary specification is now used as a spatial prior distribution in estimating the spatial distribution of dioxin concentrations on the Piazza Road pilot study area, which is part of an EPA Superfund site in Missouri. Here dioxin originally applied to the road was transported through a small stream channel at the site. Hence, the concentrations are much higher at locations near the stream channel. Also, it is expected that the spatial dependence should be stronger along the direction of the channel, which does not follow a straight path. Hence this is a case where allowing the spatial dependence to vary with location may lead to a more appropriate model.The actual pilot data contain over 1000 concentration measurements, but we use only a subset of {{formula:b0aaa3d6-4e15-4428-8bd0-2b9963986239}} data points, restricted over a subset of the pilot area as shown in Figure 3. We use {{formula:3739ba0c-0a57-4eb5-b8eb-c08388a1e645}} to denote the locations and {{formula:eb17ce56-5556-49d0-bef9-7d18fb7543e2}} to denote the log of the concentration measurements corresponding to the {{formula:4db0eb2e-8560-4f87-8490-1b984bdfbcbd}} locations. We assume the log of the dioxin concentration readings {{formula:bd79b054-3a96-4bbe-8b88-862d15bf270b}} can be decomposed into an overall mean {{formula:d18de8c7-6851-4191-985e-5b76d57e97d5}} , spatial trend {{formula:038ba93b-3d54-40d3-9072-e4ef8ffd8d2b}} , and an i.i.d. error component {{formula:1b4c9adc-5916-4d85-86d0-a05361cbb289}} so that {{formula:80d0321a-be36-447c-a12c-81e649deeda6}}We assume the errors have an i.i.d. Gaussian distribution with precision {{formula:e559d71f-e631-40b6-a302-f067b1c592e6}} . The formulation is completed by the prior specifications for {{formula:b5ff5147-770c-4a19-b950-10a49ac3f59e}} and {{formula:0399ac01-a71a-4611-b0f4-52c5b60821a7}} . For {{formula:8fe57b9f-1967-4935-bf3e-7477c3b59e7f}} we use a gamma prior; for {{formula:748bacc1-d7b4-4ac9-b78f-b96f015c8774}} we use the non-stationary Gaussian process detailed in the previous section. We give the prior specification below. {{formula:4460a5d3-bc63-4e0a-8b04-3e26e216a8c5}}The hyperparameters {{formula:58ca26d3-0377-4582-b1ef-d80b83c0b69d}} , and {{formula:c2169e4b-baa9-4518-afcb-2d39cc007e77}} are chosen to give diffuse, but proper Gamma distributions; the correlation matrix {{formula:daf2060b-d884-46e9-a762-cd647c6d5ac1}} is determined by the correlation function (REF ); the correlation matricies {{formula:ce40431e-9ee5-49c8-9ce4-fadab6b68005}} for {{formula:1b032d26-de85-4b63-820d-0baeb6c23e2b}} and {{formula:1e3ad9f4-8aad-49b3-ae6a-0b3ba3f7a7b9}} are identical and determined by the correlation function {{formula:6203cb3b-7b2b-4be5-812b-8562763353a0}} . Finally, the spatial range parameters {{formula:242c06ed-dc6b-48ae-88de-10f3fe0ab735}} and {{formula:336cdd9e-7d5b-481b-bd9d-c9cceb6971c9}} are constrained so that the resulting posterior distribution is proper. In both cases, we set {{formula:9be2b566-1419-4a22-81e0-d4a41ae4cad8}} and {{formula:a426d56c-4bfa-47d5-b047-9fef34484305}} so that any plausible value for these parameters is well within this range. {{figure:f8d0e826-9927-44bc-81bf-cf66c25bfa15}}The posterior is explored via MCMC after integrating out the {{formula:35165f64-6b45-4055-aa69-ad2e694c035d}} term. For most of the parameters, the full conditionals are not of a simple form, so stochastic simulation from the posterior is carried out primarily via Metropolis and Metropolis-Hastings steps.
RESULTS: Though the MCMC output allows one to explore many facets of the posterior distribution, we focus here on aspects pertaining to parameters which control the non-stationarity within this application. The top row of Figure 4 depicts the spatially distributed kernel estimates {{formula:fb1e5d84-25fe-4ec4-9fbb-bcc563ea956a}} at each of the data locations for {{formula:080c62b6-6fc1-4078-bb4b-db5afec5f0cf}} and 50; {{formula:6b77c9f9-8901-4857-922a-0cf161a4d4b4}} is the parameter which controls the amount of non-stationarity in the spatial correlation for {{formula:f3ff8d38-9e80-45d0-b457-d1c354896b9c}} . Each ellipse corresponds to a one standard deviation ellipse for the bivariate kernel {{formula:4b24547f-8bdb-4001-a138-a4cbcdc0bb6b}} ; each ellipse is scaled down by a factor of 4 so that it fits into the plotting region. These estimates were obtained by maximizing over {{formula:595b21d4-6c2c-4b73-af2f-b563b524a9ac}} and {{formula:99befac2-aa42-447b-a4f1-8c468c367a99}} while holding the remaining parameters at their posterior mean estimates. As expected, when {{formula:e78209a6-7975-41ea-baac-9cbe2f9b9332}} feet, a relatively small value, a fair bit of non-stationarity is present. As {{formula:f1badda6-d63e-4654-bbfa-62fb7b225c0b}} increases, the foci estimates {{formula:efe95f61-a88d-442e-b2cd-c649efbec618}} become increasingly uniform across locations. At {{formula:f57cdccc-5109-4809-a3ab-4cb58d1aaee9}} , the solution is effectively the same as in the stationary case. The resulting posterior distribution gives a 95% credible interval for {{formula:cf12c4b9-845c-405b-ad41-759c40eebe53}} of {{formula:2af802ed-1ecf-49e5-bc2a-90c843094b91}} . Hence the resulting inference for {{formula:dd9fa4fe-34d4-4e34-b10d-191996734f6d}} not only allows for non-stationarity, but also accounts for uncertainty in the degree of the departure from stationarity. Posterior mean estimates of {{formula:37c4c94a-fe99-4c3f-a8e4-c07d10046934}} at each of the data locations are depicted in the bottom rows of Figure 4. The bottom left figure shows the ellipses corresponding to the posterior mean of each pair of foci points. The bottom right figure shows the posterior mean of the actual one sd ellipses themselves where the ellipses from each MCMC realization are averaged radially. Hence, the resulting shapes are not ellipses in general. Note the posterior mean estimates show less regularity than their modal counterparts in the top row. {{figure:da9505db-c5bc-41ea-a26e-9b216a6468e2}}
DISCUSSION: We have developed a spatial process model which allows for non-stationary spatial dependence and have also given an application where MCMC is a practical and effective means of carrying out the estimation. The example presented here is unique in that it accounts for uncertainty in the extent of the non-stationarity, and it does not require repeated realizations from the spatial process. Our belief is that incorporating uncertainty due to estimating the spatial heterogeneity is important in determining whether such model extensions are worthwhile. Of course, model development is still in its initial stages and just how effective such a modeling approach may be in serious applications remains to be tested. However the initial indications are promising.Finally, we note that as with any hierarchical model specification, alternative prior formulations are possible. This is particularly true here since the nature of the models do not give rise to any inviting conjugate formulations. The spatial range parameters {{formula:42280451-a567-42ef-874f-7aa80b85c0b0}} and {{formula:c9089fc1-a0d9-448f-a38c-3419541faa27}} are especially awkward and our use of uniform prior over a fixed interval is somewhat clumsy. However the chosen intervals cover any remotely plausible range value given the application considered here. As for the spatial prior governing the {{formula:2707da7c-cf48-4554-8006-700f457535e8}} and {{formula:b71d2b31-57dd-4e18-b98b-d3815d64ac4a}} processes, our preference is for a rather simple model. One plausible alternative would be to shrink the {{formula:391f66b1-eed6-4ef0-b5a8-f50bf7aea4e9}} s towards a common {{formula:ca3e2632-1e1c-4e79-b2de-3cdf74d3a7c7}} rather than towards the origin. However, we feel that anything more elaborate is not likely to be fruitful since the data are unlikely to contain any detailed information about the structure of the {{formula:2cb27b0e-d81c-4b0d-a978-0286de0b071c}} s. Investigations regarding prior sensitivity of this approach are currently being conducted.

DH would like to thank Jerry Sacks for his insight and support during the earlier stages of the research. Thanks also to Robert Wolpert and Katja Ickstadt for many helpful discussions. First 12519 characters: Nonstationary Bayesian modeling for a large data set of derived surface temperature return values
abstract: Heat waves resulting from prolonged extreme temperatures pose a significant risk to human health globally. Given the limitations of observations of extreme temperature, climate models are often used to characterize extreme temperature globally, from which one can derive quantities like return values to summarize the magnitude of a low probability event for an arbitrary geographic location. However, while these derived quantities are useful on their own, it is also often important to apply a spatial statistical model to such data in order to, e.g., understand how the spatial dependence properties of the return values vary over space and emulate the climate model for generating additional spatial fields with corresponding statistical properties. For these objectives, when modeling global data it is critical to use a nonstationary covariance function. Furthermore, given that the output of modern global climate models can be on the order of $\mathcal{O}(10^4)$, it is important to utilize approximate Gaussian process methods to enable inference. In this paper, we demonstrate the application of methodology introduced in Risser and Turek (2020) to conduct a nonstationary and fully Bayesian analysis of a large data set of 20-year return values derived from an ensemble of global climate model runs with over 50,000 spatial locations. This analysis uses the freely available BayesNSGP software package for R.
Introduction: While the impact of anthropogenic forcings like greenhouse gas emissions on the global climate system is not yet significant or detectable for many weather and climate phenomena, the human impact on surface air temperature is well established in the literature. In recent years this influence has been documented for extreme temperature events , which can cause significant health risks for humans . Large ensembles of high-resolution global climate models are often used to study the underlying dynamical and theromdynamical aspects of extreme temperature and also quantify the anthropogenic influence on extreme temperature events, commonly termed probabilistic extreme event attribution . These large ensembles can be used to estimate quantities associated with the climatological distribution of extreme temperature, e.g., return values or return periods . However, while these derived quantities are useful on their own, it is also often important to apply a spatial statistical model to such data for several reasons: (1) to estimate return values for the grid cells where the extreme value analysis resulted in missing values, (2) to reduce the signal-to-noise ratio of the return value estimates by borrowing strength over space, (3) to understand how the spatial dependence properties of the return values vary over space, and (4) to emulate the climate model for generating additional spatial fields with corresponding statistical properties.Particularly for these latter two purposes, it is critical to utilize a nonstationary spatial statistical analysis , , , where the spatial covariance properties of the underlying process of interest are allowed to vary over the globe. However, the output of global climate models is often very large, with a {{formula:e634e7c8-6d35-4e63-a558-ec735f7e95bd}} spatial grid resulting in over 50,000 grid cells. As such, it is important to utilize approximate Gaussian process methods , , in order to avoid the computational burdens associated with evaluating the exact Gaussian process likelihood.In this paper, we utilize methodology developed by to conduct a nonstationary and fully Bayesian analysis of a large data set of estimated return values from an ensemble of global climate model runs. In Section we describe the climate model output used and the extreme value analysis used to estimate the return values. In Section we outline a Bayesian nonstationary Gaussian process model for the return values, including a full description of the nonstationary covariance function, our approach for characterizing nonstationarity, and computational details for the Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm required to fit the fully Bayesian model. Section summarizes our findings, and reproducibility code is provided in Appendix .
Data: The data used here are based on the output of an ensemble of climate model simulations from version 5.1 of the Community Atmospheric Model global atmosphere/land climate model, run in its conventional {{formula:6311bc0e-26e6-4600-8f5a-23c74a2f88b1}} 1{{formula:5a231a82-03b2-419e-9d05-57a26c6d27e5}} longitude/latitude configuration , . These simulations were run under the experiment protocols of the C20C+ Detection and Attribution Project following two climate scenarios . We utilize simulations from the “factual” (or historical) scenario, which is driven by observed boundary conditions of atmospheric chemistry (greenhouse gases, tropospheric and stratospheric aerosols, ozone), solar luminosity, land use/cover, and the ocean surface (temperature and ice coverage). The data and further details on the simulations are available at http://portal.nersc.gov/c20c; we use the 50-member ensemble that covers 01/1959 to 12/2014. A climate model ensemble is a set of runs from a particular climate model where each ensemble member has the same boundary conditions but stochastically perturbed initial conditions; the different ensemble members can be considered independent samples from the population defined by the climate model.This large ensemble of simulations is particularly suitable for evaluating climate extremes. As such, here we analyze derived maximum likelihood estimates of {{formula:13e00993-0eed-43b3-9062-6c1fde4b4349}} -year return values for the DJF seasonal mean temperature over 1960-2015. The {{formula:58cf83fe-6689-4f71-92b8-b5bee55a7ed4}} -year return value corresponds to the seasonal mean temperature value that is expected to occur once every {{formula:2dd49613-4e84-4403-a365-843635a6f56f}} years, on average (for more information, we refer the interested reader to , chapter 3). These return values are calculated as follows: first, using the 50-member ensemble of simulations, for each grid cell we first extract the ensemble maximum DJF average temperature from each year, leaving us with a sample of 56 maxima; denote these maxima as {{formula:461005f5-ffeb-44ea-89dd-186fca1354a2}} . For an individual grid cell {{formula:a30f20ab-90f8-4e2e-87c2-c0ae78ae9e3e}} , the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the {{formula:90e76a45-49f0-47de-9bff-f9a10892d294}} can be well-approximated by a member of the GEV family {{formula:e00d689a-e032-453d-849a-42a6c4d0b9e2}} , defined for {{formula:02c3df7a-1ba0-43db-a7ba-d8ab3d28f8c3}} . The GEV family of distributions (REF ) is characterized by three statistical parameters: the location parameter {{formula:2add41a0-a4a7-45b6-ad4a-40d5a3acf470}} , which describes the center of the distribution; the scale parameter {{formula:c5a42bdf-e0a5-47c9-82bf-14d5013a30d7}} , which describes the spread of the distribution; and the shape parameter {{formula:9926b287-3543-4db0-b679-12f2b124535c}} . The shape parameter {{formula:5ebe422c-52fe-4273-a0ce-eaf4cc72b1e4}} is the most important for determining the qualitative behavior of the distribution of daily rainfall at a given location. If {{formula:7262b8f0-31ec-4f21-98b6-31dae3f7a689}} , the distribution has a finite upper bound; if {{formula:6df0d7fd-7250-468c-975d-5620c3a2045d}} , the distribution has no upper limit; and if {{formula:39898972-c5dc-4b57-958e-dd09f4dd3eb8}} , the distribution is again unbounded and the CDF (REF ) is interpreted as the limit {{formula:fa05c403-b981-47b6-809f-d6fc9dc0aae4}} .Next, we fit a Generalized Extreme Value distribution to these maxima using maximum likelihood estimation (using the climextRemes package; ), resulting in estimates {{formula:c3daa78d-9bc3-4712-8962-960529cbc2cb}} for all {{formula:b4077ec9-8afd-4fbf-83a1-9fef1bd8c854}} . These MLEs can be used to calculate corresponding estimates of the DJF 20-year return value, denoted {{formula:6d589728-ab3f-4b54-9df2-aef9a6072256}} , which is defined as the DJF average temperature that is expected to be exceeded on average once every 20 years. In other words, {{formula:bed64ab9-b30f-454b-a100-d1f4bdbc69be}} is an estimate of the {{formula:aed29c01-432b-45d7-b020-696aa9ea8690}} quantile of the distribution of DJF maximum average temperature at grid cell {{formula:c0eb7c86-033a-4490-ba23-24608e2cecad}} , i.e., {{formula:e66005ef-dc91-4643-acd5-f363a5cf0292}} , which can be written in closed form in terms of the GEV parameters: {{formula:41cac51f-8ce5-4fba-86a2-2f1079fe91bc}} . The default optimization procedure in climextRemes fails for some grid cells, in which case we record a missing value; otherwise, the estimated return values are given in Kelvin (K) and are considered fixed for the remainder of the analysis (see Figure REF ; grid cells where the optimization failed are plotted in gray). The model is defined on a {{formula:60f30232-1d96-4491-9dcc-b44caec696bf}} global grid with {{formula:9cc409a0-1492-453e-b1d9-ba83e774264b}} grid cells, although we exclude the extreme pole model grid cells with a latitude of greater than {{formula:e2ec0bfb-0686-42ad-907a-d4ed030a75b1}} leaving {{formula:1a6ab68b-ca58-4d7b-962d-701738f68c4a}} cells, {{formula:02626551-d372-4da1-85b1-96c995b948e0}} of which are non-missing.
Nonstationary spatial modeling: As described in Section , a spatial model fit to these data is useful for several reasons: (1) to estimate return values for the grid cells with missing values, (2) to reduce the signal-to-noise ratio of the return value estimates by borrowing strength over space, (3) to understand how the spatial dependence properties of the return values vary over space, and (4) to emulate the climate model for generating additional spatial fields with corresponding statistical properties . When the number of nonzero elements in the Cholesky decomposition is limited to {{formula:5e79cba9-5b85-441c-8a4a-4220f6da2d0a}} (using a {{formula:8508e1c4-5c60-41bb-887f-40f8caabaef9}} nearest neighbor scheme based on maxmin ordering), the Cholesky is guaranteed to be sparse and can be calculated by solving {{formula:8cca0d70-69f9-43f1-9a8e-bb42df07073a}} linear systems of size at most {{formula:cab4f2e4-a87b-4552-94ae-27424370c5e7}} , which can be performed in {{formula:13f169d3-bf9a-4865-aa34-ce91a9699e30}} flops (furthermore, parallelization could be employed, since each linear system can be solved independently of all others). As such, the likelihood can then be calculated in {{formula:dae9e29b-a2db-4271-a547-6c3b5b019b91}} time complexity , which is linear in {{formula:91ec043d-f09e-4c4f-994c-d3f690046acf}} . Using NNGP-R, posterior prediction can only be accomplished for individual locations (also called “local kriging”) because the covariance corresponding to the prediction locations is diagonal . outline an algorithm for posterior prediction of the response (i.e., {{formula:2c30d361-3abd-4d39-908e-304c55df4bb8}} ) at a single location ; note that the same framework can be used to predict either {{formula:c198820b-ec0f-4da1-a1fe-143ecc39206d}} or {{formula:36512d7f-d4b6-4230-b082-fc84b7c851c3}} by including or not including the nugget variance, respectively, in the prediction variance.
Markov chain Monte Carlo: While this model does not contain too many parameters (12 total), it is still important to use block sampling to account for the correlated parameter space. Functionality provided by the BayesNSGP and nimble packages for R makes customizing samplers for a general MCMC straightforward. For this application, we apply a single block Metropolis Hastings sampler for the eight spatial variance coefficients {{formula:be519008-3a85-497f-84b9-336efcf0ccf9}} and another block Metropolis Hastings sampler to the two isotropy range coefficients {{formula:ef0e582a-2d43-4bf1-a4e4-9b4e0e2f214d}} . We maintain univariate adaptive random walk Metropolis Hastings samplers for the constant spatial mean and nugget variance. Looking at trace plots, the MCMC converges relatively quickly: we run the MCMC for 20,000 iterations, discarding the first 10,000 samples as burn-in and saving every 5th sample for posterior summaries and prediction. Computational times for each component of the model fitting and predictions are 37.3 hours and 13.4 hours, respectively (when running the analysis on one core of a 12-core Intel Xeon CPU E5520 machine with 128 GB memory). Note that the amount of time it takes the build and compile the model is somewhat non-trivial for this very large data set (on the order of 20 minutes). Furthermore, even with the NNGP-R likelihood, the MCMC is still somewhat slow.The code used to generate this statistical model and conduct the MCMC and prediction is provided in Appendix .
Results: The posterior mean for the overall mean is {{formula:f3ce91c8-f548-4e97-8f3b-f23a45cf6ecc}} K, with a 99% Bayesian credible interval (BCI) of {{formula:ce8a4100-0814-408b-b73d-6fa0e8bfaaf5}} ; similarly, for the overall nugget standard deviation, the posterior mean is {{formula:b0f9aeed-9a8d-4cca-a221-d5f9575db7f3}} K with a 99% BCI of {{formula:f7776ab2-1159-4024-b121-4f2847585b60}} . The posterior means for the ocean/land isotropy range are 12738 km and 1321 km, respectively (with 99% BCIs {{formula:26e73685-d5bd-4fb2-98fb-9040e602db62}} and {{formula:f68cb867-21e6-40eb-bceb-e95aa7c88b65}} ); clearly, the return values are much smoother over the ocean relative to the land. Recall, however, that the prior on the isotropy range has an upper bound of 12742 km (the diameter of the globe), such that the range over the ocean is very close to its upper bound. Finally, the zonal spatial standard deviation is shown in Figure REF . In general, ocean regions have a much smaller spatial variance relative to the land (except at the poles), with particularly small variability in the tropics (within {{formula:afe98f1b-f30d-4395-890c-c52138c5024a}} latitude), and there are significant differences between ocean and land.Next, we show the posterior predictive mean and standard deviation (both in K) in Figure REF . Unsurprisingly, given the very small estimated nugget standard deviation ({{formula:8f08bee7-d6f5-41a3-8812-35257a2f681b}} K), the predictive mean looks very similar to the raw data given in Figure REF , with one important difference: the missing values have now been filled in via the local kriging enabled by the NNGP likelihood. Interestingly, the posterior standard deviation is very clearly a function of the proximity to non-missing data values (i.e., the grid cells with a missing data value have much larger uncertainty than those with a non-missing value) but also ocean versus land. {{figure:277d3f0f-e6de-41ed-8bb6-ed429ac13fe8}}

reasoning.step1: The paper by Vinyals et al. (1612.00563) introduces Self-Critical Sequence Training (SCST), a reinforcement learning method that uses the model's own test-time inference output (e.g., greedy decoding) as a baseline to normalize rewards during training. This approach directly optimizes non-differentiable metrics like CIDEr by comparing sampled captions against the model’s own deterministic output, thereby reducing variance and improving caption quality without requiring a separate critic network.
reasoning.step2: The paper by Wang et al. (1505.01861) demonstrates that jointly modeling visual-semantic embedding — aligning the entire sentence’s semantics with video content — significantly improves caption accuracy, particularly in predicting Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) triplets. When SCST’s reward normalization mechanism (from step 1) is applied to this embedding framework, it enables the model to refine sentence generation not just locally (word-by-word) but globally (sentence-level semantics), resulting in captions that are both grammatically coherent and semantically faithful to the video content.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: Step 2 depends on Step 1 because the visual-semantic embedding framework (Wang et al.) improves caption quality by aligning sentence semantics with video content, but without a mechanism to reduce training instability and reward variance — which SCST provides — the embedding optimization is prone to noisy gradients. SCST’s use of self-critical baseline rewards stabilizes training, allowing the embedding space to be effectively learned and exploited. Neither paper alone enables this: SCST lacks semantic grounding, while the embedding model lacks reward normalization, making their combination essential for optimal performance.

questionDraft: How can reinforcement learning techniques that use a model’s own inference output as a reward baseline improve the semantic accuracy of video captions generated by models that embed sentence meaning into a joint visual-textual space?
question: How can reinforcement learning methods that normalize rewards using a model’s own deterministic output improve the semantic fidelity of video captions generated by systems that align sentence meaning with visual content through joint embedding?
answerWithPaperReferences: Reinforcement learning methods that normalize rewards using a model’s own deterministic output, such as Self-Critical Sequence Training (SCST), significantly enhance the semantic fidelity of video captions by stabilizing the training of models that embed sentence meaning into a joint visual-textual space. SCST eliminates the need for a separate critic network by using the model’s greedy-decoded caption as a baseline reward, thereby reducing variance in policy gradients and enabling more effective optimization of non-differentiable metrics like CIDEr [1612.00563]. When applied to architectures that jointly learn visual-semantic embeddings — where sentence semantics are aligned with video content through a shared embedding space — this stabilization allows the model to better refine global sentence structure and word choice based on holistic semantic relevance, rather than local word-level probabilities alone [1505.01861]. This synergy results in captions that are not only grammatically fluent but also semantically accurate, particularly in predicting Subject-Verb-Object triplets, as the embedding framework ensures that generated words correspond to true visual content, while SCST ensures that these corrections are learned efficiently and consistently during training.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: Reinforcement learning methods that normalize rewards using a model’s own deterministic output improve the semantic fidelity of video captions by stabilizing training and enabling more effective optimization of sentence-level quality metrics. By using the model’s own greedy-decoded caption as a baseline, these methods reduce reward variance and allow the system to learn which caption variations are truly superior, rather than being misled by noisy gradients. When combined with architectures that embed sentence meaning into a shared space with visual content, this approach enables the model to refine entire sentences based on global semantic alignment with the video — ensuring that subjects, verbs, and objects in the caption accurately reflect the visual scene. This results in captions that are both grammatically coherent and semantically precise, as the model learns to generate descriptions that are not just contextually plausible but also factually grounded in the video content.
isNotSingleHop: This question is not single-hop because it requires first understanding how a reinforcement learning technique (using self-critical baseline rewards) stabilizes training and reduces variance, and then combining that with the concept of visual-semantic embedding, which aligns sentence semantics with visual content. Neither mechanism alone can produce the described outcome: SCST improves training efficiency but lacks semantic grounding, while visual-semantic embedding improves semantic accuracy but suffers from training instability without reward normalization. Only by combining both — using SCST to optimize the embedding model — can the full benefit be realized, making this a true 2-hop reasoning task.
