The subscript {{formula:935e8544-a5c7-43e7-92fc-c33b0ecbafdd}} in {{formula:398a92a5-7b57-4aeb-a463-a751a5396b72}} indicates that we allow the nonlinear activation to vary on different channels. When {{formula:8daa776e-98ff-4e18-8dc1-de46a18ed07e}} , it becomes ReLU; when {{formula:17250dd5-7b32-4ca7-8255-2498ffcadcc5}} is a learnable parameter, we refer to Eqn.(REF ) as Parametric ReLU (PReLU). The motivation of LReLU is to avoid zero gradients. Experiments in show that LReLU has negligible impact on accuracy compared with ReLU. On the contrary, our method adaptively learns the PReLU parameters jointly with the whole model. The number of extra parameters is equal to the total number of channels, which is negligible when considering the total number of weights. So we expect no extra risk of overfitting. This variant only introduces a single extra parameter into each layer.

The time complexity due to PReLU is negligible for both forward and backward propagation.We adopt the momentum method when updating {{formula:7926284f-4f2d-4ef7-842f-8c4e2db4e7b7}} : {{formula:90f89ff2-375e-4e26-9edd-a00c91fb5ac9}}Here {{formula:a1d960ab-1fcf-455f-b4ab-5fb59f9ca682}} is the momentum and {{formula:d27b6e48-f532-4d55-b686-31bb2d047499}} is the learning rate. It is worth noticing that we do not use weight decay ({{formula:c7f1cf90-e172-470d-9225-676d7244fa71}} regularization) when updating {{formula:d4b98494-10fc-4d8f-b43b-28e9572a0f81}} . A weight decay tends to push {{formula:bf8ceb6d-3287-46fa-bbac-2cc60ff7262a}} to zero, and thus biases PReLU toward ReLU. Even without regularization, the learned coefficients rarely have a magnitude larger than 1 in our experiments. Further, we do not constrain the range of {{formula:5bb3e4c6-a2af-48d5-8ff1-8beb0220d190}} so that the activation function may be non-monotonic. We use {{formula:8212eef6-554f-4298-94e2-45ab72a85591}} as the initialization throughout this paper.
Comparison Experiments: We conducted comparisons on a deep but efficient model with 14 weight layers. The model was studied in (model E of ) and its architecture is described in Table REF . We choose this model because it is sufficient for representing a category of very deep models, as well as to make the experiments feasible.As a baseline, we train this model with ReLU applied in the convolutional (conv) layers and the first two fully-connected (fc) layers. The training implementation follows . The top-1 and top-5 errors are 33.82% and 13.34% on ImageNet 2012, using 10-view testing (Table REF ). {{table:c5e5730c-f8f7-44a4-8030-c3ba811bcd2b}}Then we train the same architecture from scratch, with all ReLUs replaced by PReLUs (Table REF ). The top-1 error is reduced to 32.64%. This is a 1.2% gain over the ReLU baseline. Table REF also shows that channel-wise/channel-shared PReLUs perform comparably. For the channel-shared version, PReLU only introduces 13 extra free parameters compared with the ReLU counterpart. But this small number of free parameters play critical roles as evidenced by the 1.1% gain over the baseline. This implies the importance of adaptively learning the shapes of activation functions. {{table:a0908eb4-f891-408a-b2bd-e073a475fda7}}Table REF also shows the learned coefficients of PReLUs for each layer. There are two interesting phenomena in Table REF . First, the first conv layer (conv1) has coefficients (0.681 and 0.596) significantly greater than 0. As the filters of conv1 are mostly Gabor-like filters such as edge or texture detectors, the learned results show that both positive and negative responses of the filters are respected. We believe that this is a more economical way of exploiting low-level information, given the limited number of filters (, 64). Second, for the channel-wise version, the deeper conv layers in general have smaller coefficients. This implies that the activations gradually become “more nonlinear” at increasing depths. In other words, the learned model tends to keep more information in earlier stages and becomes more discriminative in deeper stages.
Initialization of Filter Weights for Rectifiers: Rectifier networks are easier to train , , compared with traditional sigmoid-like activation networks. But a bad initialization can still hamper the learning of a highly non-linear system. In this subsection, we propose a robust initialization method that removes an obstacle of training extremely deep rectifier networks.Recent deep CNNs are mostly initialized by random weights drawn from Gaussian distributions . With fixed standard deviations (, 0.01 in ), very deep models (, {{formula:4248de45-b5bd-4c8e-b2f5-364c1c77ec8e}} 8 conv layers) have difficulties to converge, as reported by the VGG team and also observed in our experiments. To address this issue, in they pre-train a model with 8 conv layers to initialize deeper models. But this strategy requires more training time, and may also lead to a poorer local optimum. In , , auxiliary classifiers are added to intermediate layers to help with convergence.Glorot and Bengio proposed to adopt a properly scaled uniform distribution for initialization. This is called “Xavier” initialization in . Its derivation is based on the assumption that the activations are linear. This assumption is invalid for ReLU and PReLU.In the following, we derive a theoretically more sound initialization by taking ReLU/PReLU into account. In our experiments, our initialization method allows for extremely deep models (, 30 conv/fc layers) to converge, while the “Xavier” method cannot.

Architectures: The above investigations provide guidelines of designing our architectures, introduced as follows.Our baseline is the 19-layer model (A) in Table REF . For a better comparison, we also list the VGG-19 model . Our model A has the following modifications on VGG-19: (i) in the first layer, we use a filter size of 7{{formula:538fe358-d6a4-4e44-972a-92df228b526d}} 7 and a stride of 2; (ii) we move the other three conv layers on the two largest feature maps (224, 112) to the smaller feature maps (56, 28, 14). The time complexity (Table REF , last row) is roughly unchanged because the deeper layers have more filters; (iii) we use spatial pyramid pooling (SPP) before the first fc layer. The pyramid has 4 levels - the numbers of bins are 7{{formula:0c5b15be-89b7-43e6-9610-9881efae09ee}} 7, 3{{formula:e62b4f3e-b8e3-4e9a-8508-5b15c8c92993}} 3, 2{{formula:ce84644e-dbe4-4ef0-8c03-9af520d8b47b}} 2, and 1{{formula:fc70066e-a3e1-461d-b8ba-c244abcebb31}} 1, for a total of 63 bins.It is worth noticing that we have no evidence that our model A is a better architecture than VGG-19, though our model A has better results than VGG-19's result reported by . In our earlier experiments with less scale augmentation, we observed that our model A and our reproduced VGG-19 (with SPP and our initialization) are comparable. The main purpose of using model A is for faster running speed. The actual running time of the conv layers on larger feature maps is slower than those on smaller feature maps, when their time complexity is the same. In our four-GPU implementation, our model A takes 2.6s per mini-batch (128), and our reproduced VGG-19 takes 3.0s, evaluated on four Nvidia K20 GPUs.In Table REF , our model B is a deeper version of A. It has three extra conv layers. Our model C is a wider (with more filters) version of B. The width substantially increases the complexity, and its time complexity is about 2.3{{formula:618985b7-6c1c-4aa3-92da-02877c205f57}} of B (Table REF , last row). Training A/B on four K20 GPUs, or training C on eight K40 GPUs, takes about 3-4 weeks.We choose to increase the model width instead of depth, because deeper models have only diminishing improvement or even degradation on accuracy. In recent experiments on small models , it has been found that aggressively increasing the depth leads to saturated or degraded accuracy. In the VGG paper , the 16-layer and 19-layer models perform comparably. In the speech recognition research of , the deep models degrade when using more than 8 hidden layers (all being fc). We conjecture that similar degradation may also happen on larger models for ImageNet. We have monitored the training procedures of some extremely deep models (with 3 to 9 layers added on B in Table REF ), and found both training and testing error rates degraded in the first 20 epochs (but we did not run to the end due to limited time budget, so there is not yet solid evidence that these large and overly deep models will ultimately degrade). Because of the possible degradation, we choose not to further increase the depth of these large models.On the other hand, the recent research on small datasets suggests that the accuracy should improve from the increased number of parameters in conv layers. This number depends on the depth and width. So we choose to increase the width of the conv layers to obtain a higher-capacity model.While all models in Table REF are very large, we have not observed severe overfitting. We attribute this to the aggressive data augmentation used throughout the whole training procedure, as introduced below.
Training: Our training algorithm mostly follows , , , , . From a resized image whose shorter side is {{formula:ef8548c2-52c7-4ff7-8045-9fadd31afc4f}} , a 224{{formula:c79bf540-22d0-419d-aa03-753ba9c25db2}} 224 crop is randomly sampled, with the per-pixel mean subtracted. The scale {{formula:ff6e178c-6895-4f06-8579-6e66ea56d259}} is randomly jittered in the range of {{formula:a553c2c0-29a5-41fc-8280-f6617c6da8fc}} , following . One half of the random samples are flipped horizontally . Random color altering is also used.Unlike that applies scale jittering only during fine-tuning, we apply it from the beginning of training. Further, unlike that initializes a deeper model using a shallower one, we directly train the very deep model using our initialization described in Sec. REF (we use Eqn.(REF )). Our end-to-end training may help improve accuracy, because it may avoid poorer local optima.Other hyper-parameters that might be important are as follows. The weight decay is 0.0005, and momentum is 0.9. Dropout (50%) is used in the first two fc layers. The mini-batch size is fixed as 128. The learning rate is 1e-2, 1e-3, and 1e-4, and is switched when the error plateaus. The total number of epochs is about 80 for each model.
Testing: We adopt the strategy of “multi-view testing on feature maps” used in the SPP-net paper . We further improve this strategy using the dense sliding window method in , .We first apply the convolutional layers on the resized full image and obtain the last convolutional feature map. In the feature map, each 14{{formula:9ba4e06b-9f3c-4c2e-a412-fba15979933b}} 14 window is pooled using the SPP layer . The fc layers are then applied on the pooled features to compute the scores. This is also done on the horizontally flipped images. The scores of all dense sliding windows are averaged , . We further combine the results at multiple scales as in .
Multi-GPU Implementation: We adopt a simple variant of Krizhevsky's method for parallel training on multiple GPUs. We adopt “data parallelism” on the conv layers. The GPUs are synchronized before the first fc layer. Then the forward/backward propagations of the fc layers are performed on a single GPU - this means that we do not parallelize the computation of the fc layers. The time cost of the fc layers is low, so it is not necessary to parallelize them. This leads to a simpler implementation than the “model parallelism” in . Besides, model parallelism introduces some overhead due to the communication of filter responses, and is not faster than computing the fc layers on just a single GPU.We implement the above algorithm on our modification of the Caffe library . We do not increase the mini-batch size (128) because the accuracy may be decreased . For the large models in this paper, we have observed a 3.8x speedup using 4 GPUs, and a 6.0x speedup using 8 GPUs.
Experiments on ImageNet: We perform the experiments on the 1000-class ImageNet 2012 dataset which contains about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 100,000 test images (with no published labels). The results are measured by top-1/top-5 error rates . We only use the provided data for training. All results are evaluated on the validation set, except for the final results in Table REF , which are evaluated on the test set. The top-5 error rate is the metric officially used to rank the methods in the classification challenge . {{table:8ad95cf8-3b9a-4b35-b757-949124dbe966}}
Comparisons between ReLU and PReLU: In Table REF , we compare ReLU and PReLU on the large model A. We use the channel-wise version of PReLU. For fair comparisons, both ReLU/PReLU models are trained using the same total number of epochs, and the learning rates are also switched after running the same number of epochs.Table REF shows the results at three scales and the multi-scale combination. The best single scale is 384, possibly because it is in the middle of the jittering range {{formula:7fa07117-23b5-4440-b266-44b659bb6a49}} . For the multi-scale combination, PReLU reduces the top-1 error by 1.05% and the top-5 error by 0.23% compared with ReLU. The results in Table REF and Table REF consistently show that PReLU improves both small and large models. This improvement is obtained with almost no computational cost.
Comparisons of Single-model Results: Next we compare single-model results. We first show 10-view testing results in Table REF . Here, each view is a 224-crop. The 10-view results of VGG-16 are based on our testing using the publicly released model as it is not reported in . Our best 10-view result is 7.38% (Table REF ). Our other models also outperform the existing results.Table REF shows the comparisons of single-model results, which are all obtained using multi-scale and multi-view (or dense) test. Our results are denoted as MSRA. Our baseline model (A+ReLU, 6.51%) is already substantially better than the best existing single-model result of 7.1% reported for VGG-19 in the latest update of (arXiv v5). We believe that this gain is mainly due to our end-to-end training, without the need of pre-training shallow models.Moreover, our best single model (C, PReLU) has 5.71% top-5 error. This result is even better than all previous multi-model results (Table REF ). Comparing A+PReLU with B+PReLU, we see that the 19-layer model and the 22-layer model perform comparably. On the other hand, increasing the width (C B, Table REF ) can still improve accuracy. This indicates that when the models are deep enough, the width becomes an essential factor for accuracy. {{table:13ebff01-6561-4835-b877-363260b8c980}}
Comparisons of Multi-model Results: We combine six models including those in Table REF . For the time being we have trained only one model with architecture C. The other models have accuracy inferior to C by considerable margins. We conjecture that we can obtain better results by using fewer stronger models.The multi-model results are in Table REF . Our result is 4.94% top-5 error on the test set. This number is evaluated by the ILSVRC server, because the labels of the test set are not published. Our result is 1.7% better than the ILSVRC 2014 winner (GoogLeNet, 6.66% ), which represents a {{formula:1b1d8173-ac8f-46fe-ab11-053b1d613634}} 26% relative improvement. This is also a {{formula:aef70254-3216-4de4-b54e-06327f41d25a}} 17% relative improvement over the latest result (Baidu, 5.98% ). {{figure:c97e1618-5019-4eeb-ac0f-f73f4e77811a}}
Analysis of Results: Figure REF shows some example validation images successfully classified by our method. Besides the correctly predicted labels, we also pay attention to the other four predictions in the top-5 results. Some of these four labels are other objects in the multi-object images, , the “horse-cart” image (Figure REF , row 1, col 1) contains a “mini-bus” and it is also recognized by the algorithm. Some of these four labels are due to the uncertainty among similar classes, , the “coucal” image (Figure REF , row 2, col 1) has predicted labels of other bird species.Figure REF shows the per-class top-5 error of our result (average of 4.94%) on the test set, displayed in ascending order. Our result has zero top-5 error in 113 classes - the images in these classes are all correctly classified. The three classes with the highest top-5 error are “letter opener” (49%), “spotlight” (38%), and “restaurant” (36%). The error is due to the existence of multiple objects, small objects, or large intra-class variance. Figure REF shows some example images misclassified by our method in these three classes. Some of the predicted labels still make some sense.In Figure REF , we show the per-class difference of top-5 error rates between our result (average of 4.94%) and our team's in-competition result in ILSVRC 2014 (average of 8.06%). The error rates are reduced in 824 classes, unchanged in 127 classes, and increased in 49 classes. {{figure:5c1f5ee2-a6b4-4090-b00d-6d60e265717b}}
Comparisons with Human Performance from {{cite:7b4f8e9f2ecc5808499aae4ef6a5c7d9836cbb77}}: Russakovsky recently reported that human performance yields a 5.1% top-5 error on the ImageNet dataset. This number is achieved by a human annotator who is well trained on the validation images to be better aware of the existence of relevant classes. When annotating the test images, the human annotator is given a special interface, where each class title is accompanied by a row of 13 example training images. The reported human performance is estimated on a random subset of 1500 test images.Our result (4.94%) exceeds the reported human-level performance. To our knowledge, our result is the first published instance of surpassing humans on this visual recognition challenge. The analysis in reveals that the two major types of human errors come from fine-grained recognition and class unawareness. The investigation in suggests that algorithms can do a better job on fine-grained recognition (, 120 species of dogs in the dataset). The second row of Figure REF shows some example fine-grained objects successfully recognized by our method - “coucal”, “komondor”, and “yellow lady's slipper”. While humans can easily recognize these objects as a bird, a dog, and a flower, it is nontrivial for most humans to tell their species. On the negative side, our algorithm still makes mistakes in cases that are not difficult for humans, especially for those requiring context understanding or high-level knowledge (, the “spotlight” images in Figure REF ).While our algorithm produces a superior result on this particular dataset, this does not indicate that machine vision outperforms human vision on object recognition in general. On recognizing elementary object categories (, common objects or concepts in daily lives) such as the Pascal VOC task , machines still have obvious errors in cases that are trivial for humans. Nevertheless, we believe that our results show the tremendous potential of machine algorithms to match human-level performance on visual recognition. {{figure:ac838cf3-38ef-49dd-9356-670c6295bdd3}}

First 15550 characters: Safety Verification and Robustness Analysis of Neural Networks via Quadratic Constraints and Semidefinite Programming
abstract: Certifying the safety or robustness of neural networks against input uncertainties and adversarial attacks is an emerging challenge in the area of safe machine learning and control. To provide such a guarantee, one must be able to bound the output of neural networks when their input changes within a bounded set. In this paper, we propose a semidefinite programming (SDP) framework to address this problem for feed-forward neural networks with general activation functions and input uncertainty sets. Our main idea is to abstract various properties of activation functions (e.g., monotonicity, bounded slope, bounded values, and repetition across layers) with the formalism of quadratic constraints. We then analyze the safety properties of the abstracted network via the S-procedure and semidefinite programming. Our framework spans the trade-off between conservatism and computational efficiency and applies to problems beyond safety verification. We evaluate the performance of our approach via numerical problem instances of various sizes.
Introduction: Neural networks have become increasingly effective at many difficult machine-learning tasks. However, the nonlinear and large-scale nature of neural networks makes them hard to analyze and, therefore, they are mostly used as black-box models without formal guarantees. In particular, neural networks are highly vulnerable to attacks, or more generally, uncertainty in their input. In the context of image classification, for example, neural networks can be easily deluded into changing their classification labels by slightly perturbing the input image . Indeed, it has been shown that even imperceptible perturbations in the input of the state-of-the-art neural networks cause natural images to be misclassified with high probability . Input perturbations can be either of an adversarial nature , or they could merely occur due to compression, resizing, and cropping . These drawbacks limit the adoption of neural networks in safety-critical applications such as self-driving vehicles , aircraft collision avoidance procedures , speech recognition, and recognition of voice commands; see for a survey.Motivated by the serious consequences of the fragility of neural networks to input uncertainties or adversarial attacks, there has been an increasing effort in developing tools to measure or improve the robustness of neural networks. Many results focus on specific adversarial attacks and attempt to harden the network by, for example, crafting hard-to-classify examples , , , . Although these methods are scalable and work well in practice, they still suffer from false negatives. Safety-critical applications require provable robustness against any bounded variations in the input data. As a result, many tools have recently been used, adapted, or developed for this purpose, such as mixed-integer linear programming , , , , convex relaxations and duality theory , , , Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) , dynamical systems , , Abstract Interpretation , , interval-based methods , , , , . All these works aim at bounding the worst-case value of a performance measure when their input is perturbed within a specified range.Our contribution. In this paper, we develop a novel framework based on semidefinite programming (SDP) for safety verification and robustness analysis of neural networks against norm-bounded perturbations in their input. Our main idea is to abstract nonlinear activation functions of neural networks by the constraints they impose on the pre- and post- activation values. In particular, we describe various properties of activation functions using Quadratic Constraints (QCs), such as bounded slope, bounded values, monotonicity, and repetition across layers. Using this abstraction, any properties (e.g., safety or robustness) that we can guarantee for the abstracted network will automatically be satisfied by the original network as well. The quadratic form of these constraints allows us to formulate the verification problem as an SDP feasibility problem. Our main tool for developing the SDP is the {{formula:0ae4c51e-e52e-4d59-8dfe-e8876881f6f5}} -procedure from robust control , which allows us to reason about multiple quadratic constraints. Our framework has the following notable features:[leftmargin=*] We use various forms of QCs to abstract any type of activation function. Our method can capture the cross-coupling between neurons across different layers, thereby reducing conservatism. This feature, which hinges on the assumption that the same activation function is used throughout the entire network (repetition across layers), becomes particularly effective for deep networks. We can control the trade-off between computational complexity and conservatism by systematically including or excluding different types of QCs.In this paper, we focus on the neural network verification problem (formally stated in {{formula:cf627569-9ec8-404b-85f8-d325b8ab7ef0}}REF ) but the proposed framework (input-output characterization of neural networks via quadratic constraints) can be adapted to other problems such as sensitivity analysis of neural networks to input perturbations, output reachable set estimation, probabilistic verification, bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks, and closed-loop stability analysis.
Related Work: The performance of certification algorithms for neural networks can be measured along three axes. The first axis is the tightness of the certification bounds; the second axis is the computational complexity, and, the third axis is applicability across various models (e.g. different activation functions). These axes conflict. For instance, the conservatism of the verification algorithm is typically at odds with the computational complexity. The relative advantage of any of these algorithms is application-specific. For example, reachability analysis and safety verification applications call for less conservative algorithms, whereas in robust training, computationally fast algorithms are desirable , .On the one hand, formal verification techniques such as Satisfiability Modulo (SMT) solvers , , , or integer programming approaches , rely on combinatorial optimization to provide tight certification bounds for piece-wise linear networks, whose complexity scales exponentially with the size of the network in the worst-case. A notable work to improve scalability is , where the authors do exact verification of piecewise-linear networks using mixed-integer programming with an order of magnitude reduction in computational cost via tight formulations for non-linearities and careful preprocessing.On the other hand, certification algorithms based on continuous optimization are more scalable but less accurate. A notable work in this category is , in which the authors propose a linear-programming (LP) relaxation of piece-wise linear networks and provide upper bounds on the worst-case loss using weak duality. The main advantage of this work is that the proposed algorithm solely relies on forward- and back-propagation operations on a modified network, and thus is easily integrable into existing learning algorithms. In , the authors propose an SDP relaxation of one-layer sigmoid-based neural networks based on bounding the worst-case loss with a first-order Taylor expansion. The closest work to the present work is , in which the authors propose a semidefinite relaxation (SDR) for certifying robustness of piece-wise linear multi-layer neural networks. This relaxation is based on the so-called “lifting", where the original problem is embedded in a much larger space. This SDR approach provides tighter bounds than those of but is less scalable. Finally, compared to the SDR method of , our SDP framework yield tighter bounds, especially for deep networks, and is not limited to {{formula:3c1fb2f6-9353-403c-ab2c-c1be216fe8ca}} networks. Parts of this work, specialized to probabilistic verification, have appeared in the conference paper .The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In {{formula:46da7336-704f-4158-8a13-6495094a4819}} we formulate the safety verification problem and present the assumptions. In {{formula:7d12e1f2-8c59-4972-9959-365ad7501dd9}}, we abstract the problem with Quadratic Constraints (QCs). In {{formula:c7787ac0-f338-444c-9a08-5e2afc254389}} we state our main results. In {{formula:44ab9fe3-da34-4395-b25d-2f4dae6e02c4}}, we discuss further utilities of our framework beyond safety verification. In {{formula:32b02ea8-12b4-4af2-87ce-f9cee1cc80b2}} we provide numerical experiments to evaluate the performance of our method and compare it with competing approaches. Finally, in {{formula:365f5035-2c68-4b5d-9d0a-d118443da2f6}} we draw conclusions.
Notation and Preliminaries: We denote the set of real numbers by {{formula:8fb487f9-165d-4c80-abd1-ed89e64de21a}} , the set of nonnegative real numbers by {{formula:2daf32ba-bbd6-42f1-bef5-ef1e0a524953}} , the set of real {{formula:971c4dd2-e813-4970-bc56-63fcf25e7d78}} -dimensional vectors by {{formula:1a4aaf0f-4c2f-4d12-8643-e1d1dd6acb9f}} , the set of {{formula:d426bdde-e82b-45e5-8523-f3fbbdebc06c}} -dimensional matrices by {{formula:466d7117-f109-4693-93f6-6ed4df7eab87}} , the {{formula:2d2e0800-0715-48de-b249-124126ea8aa4}} -dimensional vector of all ones by {{formula:e3b14c15-8d62-44a7-8c19-77ecddc4c16f}} , the {{formula:b7a33559-231c-4364-975a-e94d83d04189}} -dimensional zero matrix by {{formula:c67ebd2e-b5d3-4cea-b6ee-735ff9503ef8}} , and the {{formula:384deff8-8a6c-4ff7-ac18-2d91ed031a75}} -dimensional identity matrix by {{formula:ed66d00b-9103-4249-b1c5-3c80d45ebc06}} . We denote by {{formula:3d445223-d6f8-421c-b7ed-772454c5b918}} , {{formula:2c7ee311-d902-4f76-a797-96fdb3fe2e39}} , and {{formula:212f5d82-5c1e-4d97-b224-8b40e1f36829}} the sets of {{formula:b35bf9e4-7968-46c6-8a28-2a80506db744}} -by-{{formula:5543b1ba-764c-403e-a74d-d1c72617bedf}} symmetric, positive semidefinite, and positive definite matrices, respectively. The {{formula:35aa561d-b751-4a17-be4b-22bd89920c74}} -norm ({{formula:b75554bb-be12-4228-94e5-a5fdafa38765}} ) is displayed by {{formula:71fd0238-7711-4168-8dae-3dc43bd5d43f}} . For {{formula:d94b15d7-06e9-43b5-a973-047f9049e6db}} , the inequality {{formula:5cc2732d-b002-4f28-a9e0-568cc3b71dc4}} is element-wise. For {{formula:cf843d48-e289-4c0b-9b8a-61804e22650d}} , the inequality {{formula:6e1bdede-a387-4ade-b3e4-87094c076e79}} means {{formula:f971bfe9-d679-463d-bcc0-602a192859eb}} is positive semidefinite. For sets {{formula:84dde817-b731-4526-abec-d053babba82e}} and {{formula:994c9361-1edc-4d4c-a615-630c17b16c92}} , we denote their Cartesian product by {{formula:af5682b2-86d3-4ebc-a0f6-40a9011d589e}} . The indicator function of a set {{formula:5b4d9a17-946e-4141-b037-55fb3ebdea7b}} is defined as {{formula:c126b184-8337-4708-ba3e-1c2396c7077b}} if {{formula:0fec656d-d5f3-4357-846a-2a4fa5122b03}} , and {{formula:f3c476c8-9275-4cf6-8d03-4aa53137161e}} otherwise. For two matrices {{formula:f5f296b3-ec01-478b-863b-e0b5978d5583}} of the same dimension, we denote their Hadamard product by {{formula:a2091fa3-7b7d-45fa-b337-2238731fbebf}} . A function {{formula:e3a34d6c-04f8-4d62-88ae-669e4470f87f}} is {{formula:acf5042e-9207-451c-bf8d-333b642e2adc}} -convex ({{formula:1dda2ac8-6ade-4f28-8e74-53f24dda3bd7}} ) if {{formula:53634616-a638-4f5c-b23d-63f96ec521ea}} is convex. Furthermore, {{formula:94a49b7b-ff44-43e2-a242-9c2b9c9f64ad}} is {{formula:0bce39f9-b54d-477f-a959-3041bceb7895}} -smooth ({{formula:9837acfd-9dfa-4670-9896-837df81934b8}} ) if it is differentiable and {{formula:0449609c-7085-4a70-9ae4-fa2b369eadf9}} is convex. Finally, if {{formula:7c21d881-a845-4454-a130-a429101ce0d6}} is {{formula:e725f778-6ea0-453c-93f6-493c2b020138}} -convex and {{formula:7e44cf8f-9d42-4414-9fcf-be4ac34a5f5a}} -smooth, then {{formula:8aa97c69-0944-4111-afd2-78aaae237ef7}}for all {{formula:b9d5b2aa-a848-4fee-81fe-c516ef2ffb15}} .
Problem Statement: Consider the nonlinear vector-valued function {{formula:2e278c09-d4cf-43e3-949f-2f69b0c1146a}} described by a multi-layer feed-forward neural network. Given a set {{formula:3df26b95-c5ea-4fcc-a116-1deb25a3a750}} of possible inputs (e.g., adversarial examples), the neural network maps {{formula:94f1b633-e9cb-45e8-8c49-7b8e2fc06318}} to an output set {{formula:33daada0-e13e-4620-b338-f34ab40e80cd}} given by {{formula:025a4960-b0e9-4646-9109-a204986ab1b7}}The desirable properties that we would like to verify can often be represented by a safety specification set {{formula:37aff2b8-9ff7-418d-805b-bc2ef9ce3875}} in the output space of the neural network. In this context, the network is safe if the output set lies within the safe region, i.e., if the inclusion {{formula:ce97cd3c-270f-4980-9df9-c590f02c2b36}} holds. Alternatively, we can define {{formula:52c8e88a-d3ce-4ab9-8c87-f32eba5cc2c6}} as the inverse image of {{formula:84b714bf-0c06-40fa-8a1b-1271fb511cd3}} under {{formula:7800d099-37cf-49d3-9843-a5c164dfd159}} . Then, safety corresponds to the inclusion {{formula:ae63c52e-1358-4af3-9177-edfddad3aa73}} .Checking the condition {{formula:82a21675-71d5-4a08-9d00-9fbdaf44d838}} , however, requires an exact computation of the nonconvex set {{formula:106dd008-d67e-49ee-b522-f250c9796522}} , which is very difficult. Instead, our interest is in finding a non-conservative over-approximation {{formula:9cb6a940-4f98-44c7-ba59-b0fad2fa9657}} of {{formula:6ae66001-657a-4ec8-ab1d-7d5faaa8ef02}} and verifying the safety properties by checking the condition {{formula:7a9d36e2-d247-4f2f-a828-a2ac47fcb604}} . This approach detects all false negatives but also produces false positives, whose rate depends on the tightness of the over-approximation–see Figure REF . The goal of this paper is to solve this problem for a broad class of input uncertainties and safety specification sets using semidefinite programming. {{figure:479f921a-c56f-466e-9e94-4e8525db894f}}
Classification Example: Consider a data (e.g., image) classification problem with {{formula:544c3456-f85d-44bf-80a0-e0c7b6963722}} classes, where a feed-forward neural network {{formula:f9d510fb-33cd-4468-a47e-a20dfcd0d629}} takes as input a data point {{formula:bd13af06-7e67-4aae-ab41-99761e41beed}} and returns an {{formula:f730facd-1502-48d8-9c9b-a671e614d0da}} -dimensional vector of scores (or logits) – one for each class. The classification rule is based on assigning {{formula:eb7f4480-d33a-4d43-a45c-adea352f203c}} to the class with the highest score. Conclusions: We proposed a semidefinite programming framework for robustness analysis and safety verification of feed-forward fully-connected neural networks with general activation functions. Our main idea is to abstract the nonlinear activation functions by quadratic constraints that are known to be satisfied by all possible input-output instances of the activation functions. We then showed that we can analyze the abstracted network via semidefinite programming. We conclude this paper with several future directions.First, a notable advantage of the proposed SDP compared to other convex relaxations is the relative tightness of the bounds. In particular, coupling all pairs of neurons in the network (repeated nonlinearities) can considerably reduce conservatism. However, coupling all neurons is not feasible for even medium-sized networks as the number of decision variables would scale quadratically with the number of neurons. Nevertheless, our numerical experiments show that most of these pair-wise couplings of neurons are redundant and do not tighten the bounds. It would be interesting to develop a method that can decide a priori that coupling which pairs of neurons would tighten the relaxation. Second, one of the drawbacks of SDPs is their limited scalability in general. Exploiting the structure of the problem to reduce the computational complexity would be an important future direction. Third, we have only considered fully-connected networks in this paper. It would be interesting to extend the results to other architectures. Finally, incorporating the proposed framework in training neural networks with desired robustness properties would be another important future direction.

questionDraft: How does the presence of a strictly positive Cheeger constant in a negatively curved planar graph conflict with the existence of a polynomially growing horosphere tower in a hyperbolic group, and why does this imply the undecidability of the domino problem for non-virtually-free hyperbolic groups?
question: When a graph exhibits a strictly positive Cheeger constant, indicating uniform exponential growth, how does this conflict with the existence of a sequence of connected, amenable graphs with polynomial growth and 2-to-1 contractions between them, and why does this geometric incompatibility imply that the domino problem is undecidable for non-virtually-free hyperbolic groups?
answerWithPaperReferences: A strictly positive Cheeger constant in a locally tessellating planar graph with negative curvature implies that the graph has exponential growth, as established by explicit lower bounds derived from combinatorial curvature constraints [0903.4793]. This exponential growth is a hallmark of hyperbolic geometry and is incompatible with the existence of a sequence of connected, amenable graphs with polynomial growth — a key component in the simulation of a hyperbolic group's Cayley graph. In particular, the construction in [2305.06952] relies on horospheres in the hyperbolic group that are connected, infinite, and exhibit uniformly polynomial growth, with contractions mapping each horosphere to the previous one in a 2-to-1 fashion. These horospheres are amenable precisely because of their polynomial growth, which is necessary for the simulation of the group's structure via a tower of graphs. However, if the ambient hyperbolic group were non-virtually-free, its global geometry would force exponential growth, contradicting the polynomial growth of the horospheres. This contradiction implies that such a simulation cannot exist unless the group is virtually free, thereby proving that the domino problem is undecidable for all non-virtually-free hyperbolic groups. The Cheeger constant from [0903.4793] thus provides the critical geometric criterion that distinguishes between polynomial and exponential growth, enabling the conclusion in [2305.06952].
answerWithoutPaperReferences: A graph with a strictly positive Cheeger constant grows exponentially, meaning the number of vertices within distance n from any point increases at an exponential rate. In contrast, a sequence of connected, amenable graphs with polynomial growth — where each graph in the sequence has a bounded number of vertices within any fixed radius — cannot coexist with exponential growth in the same ambient space. When such a polynomially growing sequence of graphs is embedded as horospheres within a hyperbolic group, with each layer mapping to the previous via a 2-to-1 contraction, it creates a simulation of the group's structure. But if the group were non-virtually-free, its global geometry would require exponential growth, directly contradicting the polynomial growth of the horospheres. This geometric incompatibility means that the simulation cannot be realized unless the group is virtually free, which in turn implies that the domino problem — the question of whether a tiling pattern can cover the entire group — cannot be algorithmically decided for non-virtually-free hyperbolic groups. The existence of a positive Cheeger constant thus serves as the decisive geometric marker that separates decidable from undecidable cases.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because it requires two distinct, sequential reasoning steps: first, recognizing that a positive Cheeger constant implies exponential growth (from the planar graph analysis), and second, understanding that this conflicts with the polynomial growth required for the horosphere tower simulation in hyperbolic groups. The conclusion — undecidability of the domino problem — depends entirely on the combination of these two results. Neither paper alone suffices: the Cheeger constant result from the first paper does not mention hyperbolic groups or the domino problem, while the hyperbolic group result from the second paper assumes polynomial growth without proving why it contradicts exponential growth. Only by combining them is the contradiction and its consequence revealed.

abstract: In this article, we study relations between the local geometry of planar graphs (combinatorial curvature) and em global geometric invariants, namely the Cheeger constants and the exponential growth. We also discuss spectral applications.
Introduction: A locally tessellating planar graph {{formula:72e052ba-4a59-4a94-aa63-03252913c38d}} is a tiling of the plane with all faces to be polygons with finitely or infinitely many boundary edges. The edges of {{formula:40dbb977-0c32-4889-938e-0f7aa151df38}} are continuous rectifiable curves without self-intersections. First 12500 characters: The domino problem for hyperbolic groups
abstract: We prove, for every non-virtually free hyperbolic group $G$, that there is no algorithm that, given a finite collection of dominoes, determines whether the Cayley graph of $G$ may be edge-covered by these dominoes so that colours match at vertices. This answers a conjecture by Aubrun, Barbieri and Moutot and goes towards settling a long-standing conjecture of Ballier and Stein.
Introduction: Consider a finitely generated group G=\langle S\rangle . The domino problem asks for an algorithm that, on input a finite set A (the “colours”) and a subset \Theta \subseteq A\times S\times A (the “dominoes”), determines whether every element of G may be coloured by A in such a manner that (\text{colour}(g),s,\text{colour}(g s))\in \Theta for all g\in G,s\in S; namely, whether the Cayley graph of G may be vertex-coloured by A in such a manner that each edge carries an allowed domino.If G admits a finite-index free subgroup, then the domino problem on G is decidable . It was conjectured by Ballier and Stein that this characterizes groups with decidable domino problem. Recall that a group G is called virtually P if the property P holds for a finite-index subgroup of G: [Ballier and Stein ] A finitely generated group has decidable domino problem if and only if it is virtually free.While this conjecture is at present (2023) still open, there has been substantial progress towards its resolution:Among finitely presented groups, the domino problem is “geometric”: if G,H are quasi-isometric then G has decidable domino problem if and only if H does. By a fundamental result of Berger , the domino problem is undecidable on ^2, and therefore on every group that contains ^2 as a subgroup. This covers all non-virtually-cyclic virtually polycyclic groups . Recall next that an action by permutations of a finitely generated group H on a group G is translation-like if it is free and acts by piecewise right-translations . If furthermore H is finitely presented and has undecidable domino problem, then G has undecidable domino problem *Theorem 3; thus every group admitting a translation-like action of ^2 has undecidable domino problem. Every infinite, finitely generated group admits a translation-like -action , so every group containing a subgroup of the form H_1\times H_2 with H_1,H_2 infinite and finitely generated has undecidable domino problem. This applies in particular to “branched groups” such as the first Grigorchuk group. The 1-skeleton of certain regular tilings of the hyperbolic plane have undecidable domino problem; from this it follows that Baumslag-Solitar groups and fundamental groups of closed surfaces have undecidable domino problem. Groups in which a graph with undecidable domino problem can be “simulated” have themselves undecidable domino problem. Loosely speaking, “simulating” means that the vertices and edges of the simulated graph are produced by an auxiliary domino problem; see §REF . The “lamplighter group” (/2)^{()}\rtimes has undecidable domino problem , since it can simulate ^2.Word hyperbolic groups were introduced by Gromov in as a common generalization of small cancellation groups and fundamental groups of negatively curved manifolds. They include fundamental groups of compact negatively curved Riemannian manifolds (such as surfaces of genus \ge 2), small cancellation groups, as well as an overwhelming proportion of finitely presented groups *§0.2A.Theorem A Let G be a word hyperbolic group. The the domino problem on G is decidable if and only if G is virtually free.See *§6 for a discussion; in particular, Gromov conjectures that every non-virtually free word hyperbolic group contains an embedded copy of a surface group, and this would imply Theorem REF . In fact, it would be enough to prove that every 1-ended (see §REF ) word hyperbolic group admits a translation-like action of a surface group. This is, however, not the approach that I follow, and these conjectures remain unfortunately open.Rather, I give a general criterion (Theorem ) that guarantees undecidability of the domino problem on a graph: it suffices to simulate a sequence (\Gamma _n)_{n\in } of connected, infinite amenable graphs and contractions \pi _n\colon \Gamma _n\rightarrow \Gamma _{n-1} (namely maps sending edges to edges or points) which are q:1 matchings for some q\in (namely every x\in \Gamma _{n-1} has precisely q preimages.). This criterion is an adaptation of Kari's proof of undecidability of the domino problem on ^2, based on the immortality problem for piecewise affine maps in the plane.This criterion subsumes all the results mentioned above: taking all the \Gamma _n\cong with \pi _n(m)=m recovers all groups that simulate the grid, while with \pi _n(m)=\lfloor m/2\rfloor recovers all groups that simulate the hyperbolic plane.I show, in §, how this criterion applies to a hyperbolic group. We first reduce to a 1-ended hyperbolic group G. The \Gamma _n are horospheres in G; they are connected because G in 1-ended, and have polynomial growth. The maps \pi _n are, suitably parameterized, the inverse of geodesic flow. A finite set of domino tiles representing the \Gamma _n and \pi _n can be recovered from a construction of an aperiodic tiling by Cohen, Goodman-Strauß and Rieck .Word hyperbolicity of a group G implies strong combinatorial properties, for example that the group has a rational growth series, and therefore that its growth rate is an algebraic number; it admits a set of normal forms for its elements that is given by a regular language. In some sense, it is possible to do even better: for example, Belk, Bleak and Matucci encode G by “asynchronous transducers” on the binary tree , and in a similar spirit Cohen, Goodman-Strauß and Rieck encode the binary (and ternary) tree into the Cayley graph of G by means of a subshift of finite type. There results seem independent, but are quite close in spirit, and simplify very much the argument.
Acknowledgments: I am very grateful to Sebastián Barbieri and Chaim Goodman-Strauss for their careful reading of a preliminary version of the manuscript, and their thoughtful remarks that helped me improve the exposition.
The domino problem: We recall the definition given in the Introduction: consider a group G with a finite generating set S. Its Cayley graph is the graph \Gamma (G,S) with vertex set G and directed edge set G\times S; the edge (g,s) starts at g, ends at g s and has label s.An instance of the domino problem on an S-edge-labeled graph \Gamma consists of a finite set A of colours and a set \Theta \subseteq A\times S\times A of tiles. One is asked to determine whether a colour can be assigned to each vertex in such a manner that for every edge (say from x to y, with label s) the triple (\text{colour}(x),s,\text{colour}(y)) belongs to \Theta .In the case of Cayley graphs — and this is the case that interests us here — this can be rephrased in terms of subshifts. Given such a \Theta , consider the spaceX_\Theta \lbrace a\in A^G:\forall s\in S,g\in G:(a(g),s,a(g s))\in \Theta \rbrace .It is a G-invariant, closed subspace of the Cantor set A^G, the G-action being given by (h\cdot a)(g)=a(h^{-1}g), and since \Theta is finite it is a typical example of subshift of finite type. The algorithmic question asked, therefore, is emptiness of subshifts of finite type given by a presentation by forbidden and allowed patterns.Yet equivalently, the set of regular subsets of X_\Theta is a Boolean algebra with G-action, and the algorithmic question asked is the triviality of G-Boolean algebras given by a finite presentation\langle \chi _a:a\in A\mid \sum _{a\in A}\chi _a=1,\quad \chi _a\chi _b=0\;\forall a\ne b,\quad \chi _a(s\cdot \chi _b)=0\;\forall (a,s,b)\notin \Theta \rangle .Decidability of the domino problem for G, or equivalently emptiness problem for G-subshifts of finite type, or triviality of finitely presented Boolean G-algebras, does not depend on the choice of S: if S^{\prime } is another generating set, every instance A,\Theta may readily be converted into an instance A^{\prime },\Theta ^{\prime } defining an isomorphic subshift.We may therefore allow or forbid “patterns” in the Cayley graph that refer to larger (but still finite) portions of the graph; and transfer “information” between any vertices at bounded distance in the Cayley graph, by reserving appropriate “slots” in the set A and transferring them edge-by-edge along any chosen path. All this “domino programming” appears confusing at first, but is quite standard and will be used without mention throughout this text.
Simulations: We recall in simplified form the definition of simulations from . We consider vertex- and edge-colourings specified on an edge-labeled graph \Gamma , and say that \Gamma simulates a graph \Delta if there is a set of domino tiles for \Gamma whose solutions have the following properties:they specify at each vertex v\in \Gamma a collection of marked vertices (v,i)_{0<i\le m(v)} and a collection of unmarked vertices (v,-i)_{0\le i< u(v)}; they specify at each edge in \Gamma , say joining v to w, a subgraph of the complete bipartite graph on \lbrace (v,i):-u(v)<i\le m(v)\rbrace \times \lbrace (w,j):-u(w)<j\le m(w)\rbrace ; the graph \Delta is isomorphic to the graph with vertex set \lbrace (v,i):v\in \Gamma ,0<i\le m(v)\rbrace and an edge from (v,i) to (w,j) whenever there is a sequence of edges from (v,i) to (w,j) in the bipartite graphs, that traverses only unmarked vertices except at its endpoints.There are numerous variants of the definition: the graph \Delta may be oriented, unoriented, or edge-labeled (in which case the simulation must specify the edge labels). Rather than simulating one graph, we simulate a closed space of graphs, namely the family of all graphs whose finite subgraphs belong to a specified collection; see *§3.2 for a discussion. The main point is: [*Theorem 3.7] If \Gamma simulates \Delta and \Delta has undecidable domino problem, then so does \Gamma .Note that, if \Delta is the Cayley graph of a finitely presented group, “simulating \Delta ” is a weaker notion than “admitting a quasi-isometric embedding of \Delta ” or “admitting a translation-like action of \Delta ”: indeed in a simulation the edges of \Delta are represented by regular patterns of edges in \Gamma rather than by edges of bounded length.
Towers of graphs: A tower of graphs consists of a sequence (\Delta _n)_{n\in } of graphs and a sequence (\pi _n\colon \Delta _n\rightarrow \Delta _{n-1})_{n\ge 1} of graph contractions (namely maps that send edges to edges or points). It is connected, bounded-degree, amenable (see below), etc. if every \Delta _n has this property. For q\in , it is q-regular if every vertex in every \Delta _n has exactly q preimages under \pi _{n+1}. The graphs \Delta _n may be oriented, unoriented, edge-labeled, etc.; in our applications, they will be unoriented, simple graphs.For a graph \Gamma , we keep the notation \Gamma for its vertices, and write E(\Gamma ) for its set of edges, each of which is an unordered pair of vertices. For a set A\subseteq \Gamma of vertices, recall that its boundary \partial A is the set of edges of \Gamma that have precisely one endpoint in A, and its neighbourhood N(A) is the set of vertices that either belong to A or are connected to A by an edge. The graph \Gamma is amenable if it admits a Følner sequence: a sequence (F_k)_{k\in } of non-empty finite subsets of \Gamma withk\#(\partial F_k)\le \#F_k\text{ for all }k\in .For example, if balls grow subexponentially in \Gamma , then a subsequence of them will constitute a Følner sequence.A tower of graphs (\Delta _n)_{n\in } may be viewed as a special kind of graph \Delta , in which edges come in two flavours: “vertical” oriented edges, and “horizontal” edges of the same type as those of the \Delta _n. reasoning.step1: The paper quant-ph/0611063 establishes that the algebra of 15 generalized Pauli operators for two-qubit systems is isomorphic to the geometry of a projective line over the non-commutative ring of 2×2 matrices over GF(2). This geometry is equivalent to a generalized quadrangle of order two, where points represent operators and the relation of being 'distant' or 'neighbor' corresponds to non-commuting or commuting operators, respectively. Crucially, it identifies that the maximum set of five mutually non-commuting operators corresponds to an 'ovoid' in this geometry, which is a set of five points where no two are neighbors (i.e., no two commute).
reasoning.step2: The paper 1107.3050 demonstrates that in certain rings — specifically those with at least two maximal right ideals, at least one of which is non-principal — there exist vectors that are not generated by any unimodular vector (called 'outliers') and yet still generate free cyclic submodules (FCSs). These FCSs generated by non-unimodular vectors are precisely the algebraic structures that correspond to sets of operators that are mutually non-commuting but cannot be generated from any set of commuting (unimodular) operators. Combining this with the geometric identification from quant-ph/0611063, the ovoid (five mutually non-commuting operators) must be generated by a non-unimodular vector, because if it were generated by a unimodular vector, it would contradict the structure of the generalized quadrangle where such a set cannot be embedded in any FCS generated by unimodular vectors alone.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: Step 1 provides the geometric structure (generalized quadrangle) and identifies the ovoid as a maximal set of five mutually non-commuting operators. Step 2 provides the algebraic condition under which such a set can be generated by a non-unimodular vector. The connection is essential because the ovoid (from Step 1) cannot be generated by any unimodular vector (as proven in quant-ph/0611063), yet it is a valid FCS — which only occurs if the underlying ring has non-principal maximal ideals (as proven in 1107.3050). Thus, the existence of the ovoid as a valid FCS depends on the ring structure described in 1107.3050; without knowing that non-unimodular vectors can generate FCSs, the ovoid would appear as an anomaly in the geometry. The two steps are inseparable: the geometric object (ovoid) only makes sense as a legitimate FCS if the algebraic condition (non-principal ideals enabling non-unimodular FCSs) holds.

questionDraft: In the geometric representation of two-qubit operators as points in a generalized quadrangle of order two, what algebraic property of the underlying ring ensures that the maximum set of five mutually non-commuting operators forms a free cyclic submodule generated by a non-unimodular vector?
question: In the geometric representation of two-qubit operators as points in a generalized quadrangle of order two, what algebraic property of the underlying ring ensures that the maximum set of five mutually non-commuting operators forms a free cyclic submodule generated by a non-unimodular vector?
answerWithPaperReferences: The maximum set of five mutually non-commuting operators in the two-qubit system corresponds to an ovoid in the generalized quadrangle of order two, as established by the isomorphism between the operator algebra and the projective line over the non-commutative ring of 2×2 matrices over GF(2) [quant-ph/0611063]. This ovoid cannot be generated by any unimodular vector, as unimodular vectors generate free cyclic submodules that are constrained by the commutation structure of commuting operators, which do not span such maximal non-commuting sets. However, the existence of such an ovoid as a legitimate free cyclic submodule (FCS) is only possible if the underlying ring possesses at least two maximal right ideals, at least one of which is non-principal [1107.3050]. This algebraic condition allows for the existence of non-unimodular vectors that generate FCSs, which are precisely the vectors corresponding to the ovoid. Thus, the ovoid as an FCS is not merely a geometric curiosity but a direct consequence of the ring's non-principal ideal structure, which permits the generation of FCSs from non-unimodular vectors — a phenomenon that does not occur in rings where all ideals are principal or where only one maximal ideal exists.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: In the geometric representation of two-qubit operators as points in a generalized quadrangle of order two, the maximum set of five mutually non-commuting operators forms a structure known as an ovoid. This set cannot be generated from any set of commuting operators (which correspond to unimodular vectors), yet it still constitutes a valid free cyclic submodule. For this to occur, the underlying algebraic structure must allow for the generation of such submodules by non-unimodular vectors. This is only possible when the ring has at least two maximal right ideals, and at least one of them is not generated by a single element (i.e., is non-principal). This algebraic condition enables the existence of vectors that are not derived from invertible elements but still generate complete submodules, thereby allowing the ovoid — a maximal set of non-commuting operators — to emerge as a legitimate algebraic object within the geometry.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because it requires first identifying the ovoid as a maximal set of five mutually non-commuting operators within the generalized quadrangle geometry (from quant-ph/0611063), and then recognizing that such a set can only be generated as a free cyclic submodule if the underlying ring has non-principal maximal ideals (from 1107.3050). Neither paper alone suffices: quant-ph/0611063 describes the geometric structure but does not explain how such a set is algebraically generated, while 1107.3050 describes the algebraic condition for non-unimodular FCSs but does not connect it to the specific geometric object (ovoid) in the two-qubit system. Only by combining both can one conclude that the ovoid's existence as an FCS depends on the ring's non-principal ideal structure.
bridgeEvidencePaperText:
Projective Ring Line Encompassing Two-Qubits
abstract: The projective line over the (non-commutative) ring of two-by-two matrices with coefficients in GF(2) is found to fully accommodate the algebra of 15 operators - generalized Pauli matrices - characterizing two-qubit systems. The relevant sub-configuration consists of 15 points each of which is either simultaneously distant or simultaneously neighbor to (any) two given distant points of the line. The operators can be identified with the points in such a one-to-one manner that their commutation relations are exactly reproduced by the underlying geometry of the points, with the ring geometrical notions of neighbor/distant answering, respectively, to the operational ones of commuting/non-commuting. This remarkable configuration can be viewed in two principally different ways accounting, respectively, for the basic 9+6 and 10+5 factorizations of the algebra of the observables. First, as a disjoint union of the projective line over GF(2) x GF(2) (the "Mermin" part) and two lines over GF(4) passing through the two selected points, the latter omitted. Second, as the generalized quadrangle of order two, with its ovoids and/or spreads standing for (maximum) sets of five mutually non-commuting operators and/or groups of five maximally commuting subsets of three operators each. These findings open up rather unexpected vistas for an algebraic geometrical modelling of finite-dimensional quantum systems and give their numerous applications a wholly new perspective.

These findings open up rather unexpected vistas for an algebraic geometrical modelling of finite-dimensional quantum systems and give their numerous applications a wholly new perspective.MSC Codes: 51C05, 51E12, 81R99, 81Q99PACS Numbers: 02.10.Hh, 02.40.Dr, 03.65.CaKeywords: Projective Ring Lines – Generalized Quadrangle of Order Two – Two-QubitsProjective lines defined over finite associative rings with unity/identity{{formula:c374f494-4d34-4ba6-98f9-feb14a226315}} have recently been recognized to be an important novel tool for getting a deeper insight into the underlying algebraic geometrical structure of finite dimensional quantum systems.{{formula:536aae46-c0fc-4778-8e68-4f3adade3c2a}} Focusing almost uniquely on the two-qubit case, i.e., the set of 15 operators/generalized four-by-four Pauli spin matrices, of particular importance turned out to be the lines defined over the direct product of the simplest Galois fields, {{formula:8350b8d6-39bb-4c61-af40-c98952c5a8aa}} . Here, the line defined over {{formula:a559f1c5-b989-48da-995a-1c62a303d24d}} plays a prominent role in grasping qualitatively the basic structure of so-called Mermin squares,{{formula:6439e7df-724c-464d-8711-7feacd3e9ea2}} i. e., three-by-three arrays in certain remarkable 9 + 6 split-ups of the algebra of operators, whereas the line over {{formula:1a581476-845f-4576-9a8b-39cb3868ea46}} reflects some of the basic features of a specific 8 + 7 (“cube-and-kernel") factorization of the set.{{formula:89244e6a-2ce7-4987-bffe-94239f9520fc}} Motivated by these partial findings, we started our quest for such a ring line that would provide us with a complete picture of the algebra of all the 15 operators/matrices. The first is simply a disjoint union of the projective line over {{formula:a19354e7-55f6-4b57-9208-38fa9c74a611}} and two lines over {{formula:ab85dec5-fe8b-4053-b523-551a1e39981d}} passing through the two selected points {{formula:6d0473bb-439e-4cf6-a65f-a0d91321ed45}} and {{formula:b23dc123-32af-4925-9591-6ac50bfad8f9}} , these latter omitted. As demonstrated in detail elsewhere,{{formula:9f747341-2c37-43ef-a730-e9a5d488b56f}} the line over {{formula:6497f7e3-9dd1-4016-a858-c769e4e61222}} underlies the qualitative structure of Mermin's magic squares, i. e., {{formula:c4ee34f5-08b4-48fd-9f58-cdc2e225b41a}} arrays of nine observables commuting pairwise in each row and column and arranged so that their product properties contradict those of the assigned eigenvalues. The two lines over {{formula:5576d36a-9ef5-40f3-a23e-8ad3a125720a}} represent the remaining, bipartite part of the split-up, where three points/observables on each of the lines are mutually distant/non-commuting and every point/observable of one line is neighbor to/commutes with any point/observable of the other line (see Fig. 1, left). {{figure:81132fec-f10a-4749-8a51-bb41171eafbb}}The second interpretation involves a generalized quadrangle, a rank two point-line incidence geometry where two points share at most one line and where for any point {{formula:836d0892-3f97-4016-9196-69c0fcae7a77}} and a line {{formula:c0e2318a-f5c0-417a-aeea-8ddce164b72b}} , {{formula:ce03e0d1-1340-4aa7-ad78-1a926a9da524}} , there exists exactly one line through {{formula:0d116802-f8e0-4f0a-bb55-175e7bf26a97}} which intersect {{formula:06f46024-f48e-482b-ae4a-6cbf286c3e24}} .{{formula:1dfaa426-7b63-4262-a7d4-2150bdaf9d5b}} The generalized quadrangle associated with our observables is of order two, i. e., the one where every line contains three points and every point is on three lines. Such a quadrangle has, indeed, 15 points (and, because of its self-duality, the same number of lines), each of which is joined by a line with other six (Fig. 2, left). If one removes from this quadrangle one of its ovoids, i. e., a set of (five) points that has exactly one point in common with every line (Fig. 2, middle), one is left with the set of ten points that form the famous Petersen graph (Fig. 2, right);{{formula:4001c0b9-45c6-4007-94f6-d138d7de63f0}} five points of an ovoid answer to nothing but the five mutually distant points of {{formula:a7122ee8-1cd2-4c76-989c-40c113590bfc}} and, so, to the five (i. e., the maximum number of) mutually non-commuting observables of two-qubits. If, dually, one removes from the quadrangle a spread, i. e., a set of (five) pairwise disjoint lines that partition the point set, one gets the dual of the Petersen graph (Fig. 3); five lines of a spread represent nothing but the five maximum subsets of three mutually commuting operators each, whose associated bases are mutually unbiased.{{formula:d72628ba-a86f-448c-a760-4b0e34529817}} It is a straightforward exercise to associate the points of the quadrangle with the operators/observables {{formula:83d7a38d-86cd-45dc-b6e4-f8678f59af89}} , Eq. (8), in such a way to recover Table 2, after substituting the “{{formula:fd6b40d4-0e70-4820-ae19-621a0d9f46e2}} "/“{{formula:1999196a-ba70-4323-861f-aeb4b0af22e5}} " sign for any two points of the quadrangle which are/are not on a common line. {{figure:12d0e7c6-7843-4a89-93a9-c4522de4679c}}{{figure:8598dad9-e404-45d0-8063-3514f897f044}}To complete this interesting algebraic geometrical picture of two-qubits there remains to be introduced one more important geometrical object. The attentive reader might have noticed that we have already employed two different kinds of the projective lines defined over rings of order four and characteristic two, viz. the line defined over the field {{formula:9036e413-aefe-46d7-ae7e-e383c56295dc}} and that defined over the direct product ring {{formula:3a59da91-9f8d-443a-8178-9a78785c8101}} ; the former was seen to answer to an ovoid of the generalized quadrangle, alias to a set of five mutually non-commuting operators (Fig. 1, right – top), while the latter corresponds to a grid of nine points on six lines,Also known as the slim generalized quadrangle of order ({{formula:2273a3dc-8d01-4b42-ac40-8c68503b47e1}} ); see, e. g., Refs. 18 and 20. In fact, both the configurations depicted in Fig. 1, left, are slim generalized quadrangles, one being the dual of the other. alias to a Mermin's square of operators (Fig. 1, left – bottom). There, however, exists one more associative ring with unity of order four and characteristic two, namely the (local) factor ring of polynomials {{formula:c11ecb36-de50-4e88-a028-385aac8c97f9}} .{{formula:e4efdef3-3758-459f-b457-8091a64ecac1}} This ring is also a subring of {{formula:f0f96547-8081-4400-a296-d7d48339502d}} , so the corresponding projective line is expected to play a role in our model, too. And this is indeed the case. As demonstrated, for example, in Ref. 6 (Table 3), the projective line {{formula:ba798ac9-e6b6-4b83-b817-4fa787666501}} features six points any of which is neighbor to one and distant to the remaining four points, comprising thus three pairs of neighbors. In the set of Pauli operators this configuration is present as the sextuple of operators commuting with a given operator; taking the latter to be, e. g., {{formula:7cb769f9-bb0e-465d-b9bf-959e3337ac45}} , the six operators in question, as readily discerned from Table 2, are {{formula:598dc6ee-369b-47e9-9aba-d91293974dbf}}{{formula:9b86e7c1-9c0c-4c9d-b5de-72929be3423d}} , {{formula:e1ff5202-1a77-4b5d-bfd3-ca8b66c2fb5e}} ; {{formula:56ea43c7-8c2b-4faf-8ac2-b7e55105c6e9}} , {{formula:0779905d-f7ea-41f9-99c8-04c66a359a95}} ; {{formula:dedd2518-08c8-40ba-a3ef-5d22987a764a}} , {{formula:d2ad4e59-b7d0-4d8e-9986-fbc88950068f}}{{formula:915a990b-ed42-4ab8-9b52-5f06bde30e4e}} , which indeed form three pairs of commuting members (these pairs being separated from each other by a semicolon). In the generalized quadrangle any such configuration resides as the sextuple of points collinear with a given point. A deeper understanding and a fuller appreciation of this observation is acquired after introducing the concept of a geometric hyperplane. A geometric hyperplane {{formula:7a63b30d-c858-4e5e-b7c6-6e95e9be888c}} of a finite geometry is a set of points such that every line of the geometry either contains exactly one point of {{formula:33eddd3f-e14d-403b-b9b6-2c94f47b77b3}} , or is completely contained in {{formula:50ae501a-519d-47b5-9e6b-424d4f21b920}} .{{formula:8ca2d287-551c-494f-9e7e-80c5865d9805}} It is easy to verify that for the generalized quadrangle of order two {{formula:5c07cd05-72dc-49a6-aa8c-084257925314}} is of one of the following three kinds:{{formula:e6e1bafe-632b-40e1-9cbf-e39d824e750b}} 1) {{formula:376f6b8e-028d-4867-836f-dedf26f305e1}} , an ovoid (there are six such hyperplanes); 2) {{formula:27edcbb9-6f15-49c0-ab09-f4cbd71b0164}} , a set of points collinear with a given point {{formula:3ce2104c-f1a3-407f-b77c-03b2c62ac523}} , the point itself inclusive (there are 15 such hyperplanes); and 3) {{formula:600e043f-820f-4437-b495-1e74fd1800e9}} , a grid as defined above (there are 10 such hyperplanes). One thus reveals a perfect parity between the three kinds of the geometric hyperplanes of the generalized quadrangle of order two and the three kinds of the projective lines over the rings of four elements and characteristic two embedded in our sub-configuration of {{formula:1c11e311-aba8-41f7-a3d2-7ddf69bde359}} , giving rise to the three kinds of the distinguished subsets of the Pauli operators of two-qubits, as summarized in Table 3. {{table:e6bb8ac9-892d-4210-8822-9f2aa6ef191d}}As a final note, it is worth mentioning that the generalized quadrangle of order two also resides in {{formula:ab0723c8-38dd-4bb7-84c2-1cc2a6af0145}} as the projective line over the so-called Jordan system of symmetric two-by-two matrices over {{formula:9472280f-cc17-4f1e-8f05-b577d4ae1b59}} ,{{formula:1cc3d7d6-6f96-4364-9fcb-4424aa410ca7}} or, equivalently, as a generic hyperplane section of the Klein quadric in the 5-dimensional projective space over {{formula:c44fff36-3147-4353-8f8c-2aca851163fa}} .{{formula:f634bab5-28cd-4193-aa91-d6235dae19df}}We have demonstrated that the basic properties of a system of two interacting spin-1/2 particles are uniquely embodied in the (sub)geometry of a particular projective line, found to be equivalent to the generalized quadrangle of order two. As such systems are the simplest ones exhibiting phenomena like quantum entanglement and quantum non-locality and play, therefore, a crucial role in numerous applications like quantum cryptography, quantum coding, quantum cloning/teleportation and/or quantum computing to mention the most salient ones, our discovery thus not only offers a principally new geometrically-underlined insight into their intrinsic nature, but also gives their applications a wholly new perspective and opens up rather unexpected vistas for an algebraic geometrical modelling of their higher-dimensional counterparts.{{formula:4725a3ef-abf9-4b01-b43f-0edcd4b0fe8f}}AcknowledgementsThe first author thanks Prof. Hans Havlicek (Vienna University of Technology) for bringing to our attention the description of the generalized quadrangle of order two as the projective line over the Jordan system of the ring in question. This work was partially supported by the Science and Technology Assistance Agency under the contract {{formula:96f0da68-0524-48aa-88b0-c38d904aaf51}} APVT–51–012704, the VEGA project {{formula:4b5e5dcd-0a88-4bc2-ab60-75deff9c786a}} 2/6070/26 (both from Slovak Republic), the trans-national ECO-NET project {{formula:70965028-ce75-4a3d-887f-dd9b86144d20}} 12651NJ “Geometries Over Finite Rings and the Properties of Mutually Unbiased Bases" (France) and by the project 1ET400400410 of the Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic.

First 12634 characters: Free Cyclic Submodules and Non-Unimodular Vectors
abstract: Given a finite associative ring with unity, $R$, and its two-dimensional left module, $^{2}R$, the following two problems are addressed: 1) the existence of vectors of $^{2}R$ that do not belong to any free cyclic submodule (FCS) generated by a unimodular vector and 2) conditions under which such (non-unimodular) vectors generate FCSs. The main result is that for a non-unimodular vector to generate an FCS of $^{2}R$, $R$ must have at least two maximal right ideals of which at least one is non-principal.
Introduction: Projective geometries over finite associative rings with unity have recently found important applications in coding theory (see, e. g., ) and quantum information theory (see, e. g., , , ). When constructing a geometry over a ring, a majority of authors consider as points of such a geometry only free cyclic submodules (FCSs) generated by unimodular vectors , whilst some authors consider all cyclic submodules , . It has recently been shown that there exists rings for which some vectors of the submodule are not contained in an FCS generated by a unimodular vector. These vectors have been called outliers. Even more interesting is that some outliers themselves generate FCSs. A geometry may be constructed using all FCSs.Analysing all finite associative rings with unity up to order 31 inclusive, only several rings are found to feature outliers. Out of these, only few non-commutative rings exhibit FCSs comprising solely non-unimodular vectors ; the smallest example being the ring of ternions over the Galois field of order two . These examples motivated a more systematic and general treatment of the questions of the existence of outliers and FCSs generated by them. The outcomes of our explorations are not only interesting on their own, but they can also have interesting physical bearings (like, e. g., those proposed in ).
Definitions and Preliminaries : All rings considered are finite, associative and with unity (multiplicative identity). It is well known that in such a ring, {{formula:f3ec4ac7-649b-4855-835f-78033d46fb3d}} , an element is either a unit or a (two-sided) zero-divisor (see, for example, ); in what follows the group of units of {{formula:f177174f-cecc-4998-9c78-0b1d698aeff8}} is denoted by {{formula:899a70cb-765d-454b-8313-6aa710a95ae5}} and the set of zero divisors by {{formula:0092b877-bf59-407a-b9fd-2bc2dc5ce2c3}} . 1 is the unity element of {{formula:046a2c82-5370-430e-a3b5-faed482dd577}} and the symbol {{formula:af5eeb2d-8cd6-44fa-9bee-99f966f5ff40}} stands for strict inclusion.Definition 1 Let {{formula:3c1bf71e-82c3-4100-ad76-548e95a27c30}} be a ring. A left ideal, {{formula:ee21d693-9520-4f26-bbdb-7bbceb35164a}} , is a subgroup of {{formula:e0763261-3ffe-480b-b94a-94baedfba01f}} such that {{formula:62d13402-99e5-4fcc-b420-6588e9df2ca7}} for all {{formula:66d0ab6b-9e3a-4033-b67d-0d270a438db5}} and {{formula:b1628bdc-a99a-472e-b9ab-882e48d0d530}} . A right ideal, {{formula:0c435880-6f90-4c87-91d2-f33bdc385a52}} , is a subgroup of {{formula:bc13dd5b-5c4f-4b35-84ab-77664e6163d3}} such that {{formula:8d10a2a8-6161-4c70-8b96-1cac40a7a1e4}} for all {{formula:7364473d-266b-45c8-929c-cb45e7df730e}} and {{formula:3efcd3a4-cdf3-4715-bb8f-b0ea498b1bf8}} . Conclusion and Further Directions: For the existence of FCSs of {{formula:4bf502e8-a919-4619-9cde-30256f6c3f66}} that are generated by non-unimodular vectors (“non-unimodular FCSs"), {{formula:27992a32-18b3-463d-be09-9b9ad8e3b68b}} must have at least two maximal right ideals, at least one of which is non-principal. This is a necessary condition. Calculated examples show that this condition is not sufficient; other properties of a ring are required to guarantee the presence of FCSs generated by non-unimodular vectors.As already mentioned in the introduction, in our worked examples non-unimodular FCSs have been only found for non-commutative rings. One would be tempted to conjecture that non-commutativity is essential in this respect. Yet, this is questionable because some rings feature non-unimodular FCSs in {{formula:05f73bd2-b49a-48f3-b863-d42bec174295}} , but not in {{formula:1a8a2320-3e8b-4310-8737-0614e524d84d}} (and vice versa). Hence, it is highly desirable to clarify to what extent the existence of non-unimodular FCSs depends on the non-commutativity of the ring; in particular, what is the smallest commutative ring featuring non-unimodular FCSs?Further, in all analysed examples, a non-unimodular FCS was found to share with any other FCS at least one vector apart from {{formula:10c06c83-dcc9-4f78-a3ee-ab0171f5fa36}} ; is this true in general, or just a feature of the particular small-order rings? Finally, within our bank of examples, we found rings where all outliers generate FCSs (like the smallest ring of ternions ), as well as rings where only some outliers have this property. What distinguishes the two kinds of rings? These are exciting open questions we would like to focus on in the near future.
